stories.title: 📊 Numbers 1
summaryBullets: On the first day of the second month of the second year after the Israelites had come out of the land of Egypt, the LORD spoke to Moses in the Tent of Meeting in the Wilderness of Sinai. He said: (1:1).
“Take a census of the whole congregation of Israel by their clans and families, listing every man by name, one by one. (1:2).
You and Aaron are to number those who are twenty years of age or older by their divisions— everyone who can serve in Israel’s army. (1:3).
And one man from each tribe, the head of each family, must be there with you. (1:4).
These are the names of the men who are to assist you: From the tribe of Reuben, Elizur son of Shedeur; (1:5).
from Simeon, Shelumiel son of Zurishaddai; (1:6).

from Benjamin, Abidan son of Gideoni; (1:11).

from Asher, Pagiel son of Ocran; (1:13).

These men were appointed from the congregation; they were the leaders of the tribes of their fathers, the heads of the clans of Israel. (1:16).
So Moses and Aaron took these men who had been designated by name, (1:17).

And all those counted totaled 603,550. (1:46).
The Levites, however, were not numbered along with them by the tribe of their fathers. (1:47).
For the LORD had said to Moses: (1:48).

Instead, you are to appoint the Levites over the tabernacle of the Testimony, all its furnishings, and everything in it. They shall carry the tabernacle and all its articles, care for it, and camp around it. (1:50).

The Israelites are to camp by their divisions, each man in his own camp and under his own standard. (1:52).

But the Levites are to camp around the tabernacle of the Testimony and watch over it, so that no wrath will fall on the congregation of Israel. So the Levites are responsible for the tabernacle of the Testimony.” (1:53).
Thus the Israelites did everything just as the LORD had commanded Moses. (1:54).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׂאוּ אֶת-רֹאשׁ (se'u et-rosh), lift the head
translationNotes.note: The Hebrew idiom is lift up the head of the congregation, meaning to take a headcount. This is a military muster, not a population survey: the criterion in verse 3 is every male twenty years old and upward who is able to go out to war, so it counts no women, no children and no men over military age. Exodus 30:12-16 attaches a half shekel payment to being counted, which is why the same figure of 603,550 turns up as a silver total in Exodus 38:26.

The same Hebrew word does duty for the number one thousand and for a clan or a military contingent led by one man. Gideon protests that his eleph is the weakest in Manasseh (Judges 6:15), Samuel musters Israel by tribes and by their alaphim (1 Samuel 10:19), and Micah 5:2 calls Bethlehem little among the alphei of Judah, where a number makes no sense. A reader should know that the word in these totals carries both senses, and that the same word underlies the ranks called commanders of thousands.

A tribal standard, a pole with an emblem carried at the head of a division so that men could find their unit in a camp of this size and keep formation on the march. Assyrian and Egyptian armies used exactly such standards, shown on their reliefs. Chapter 2 sets out which tribes camped under which of the four, and 10:14-28 gives the marching order they moved in.

Mishkan means a dwelling, from the verb to settle down, and it names the portable sanctuary: a wooden frame hung with woven curtains, taken apart and reassembled at every stop. The Testimony is the two stone tablets kept inside the ark (Exodus 25:16). The whole camp in chapter 2 is laid out as a square around this one tent, with the Levites forming a ring between it and everyone else.

stories.keyTakeaway: God directs Moses and Aaron to take a census of all Israelite men twenty years and older fit for military service, enlisting twelve tribal leaders to assist; the total count reaches 603,550. The Levites are excluded from this census and instead assigned to care for the tabernacle and its furnishings.

and his division numbers 53,400. (2:30).

crossRefs: Numbers 10:14-28: The same four divisions listed again in the order they actually broke camp and marched.
Exodus 13:21-22: The pillar of cloud by day and fire by night goes ahead of the camp to lead the way.

Revelation 21:12-13: Twelve gates, three on the east, three on the north, three on the south and three on the west.

translationNotes.note: Machaneh means both an encampment and an army division, which is why the four groups here are called camps. The layout is a square: three tribes on each side, the Levites in an inner ring around the tent, and the tent at the centre. Egyptian war camps were pitched the same way, with the pharaoh's tent in the middle of a rectangle of troops, as shown in the reliefs of the Battle of Kadesh.

The ordinary tribes camp facing the tent but set back from it, with the Levites filling the gap. It is a security cordon, and 1:51 states the reason: any outsider who comes near is to be put to death. Joshua 3:4 sets the distance for the ark on the march at about two thousand cubits, roughly 900 metres.

The order is fixed and it matters later. Judah leads on the east, Reuben follows on the south, then the tent itself in the middle of the column, then Ephraim on the west, and Dan brings up the rear on the north (2:9,16,18,25). Judah in the vanguard and Dan as rear guard is the same arrangement Israel keeps in Judges 1:1-2, where Judah is sent up first.

The four divisions total 186,400 for Judah, 151,450 for Reuben, 108,100 for Ephraim and 157,600 for Dan, and those add to the 603,550 of 1:46. A camp of that size with families and livestock is a moving city, which is what Balak sees at 22:3 and what makes Moab's fear in that verse a practical calculation rather than superstition.

stories.keyTakeaway: God commands Moses and Aaron to organize the Israelites in a specific camp arrangement around the tent of meeting, with twelve tribes grouped into four divisions on the east, south, west, and north, each under assigned leaders and numbered at 603,550 men total.

stories.title: 📊 Numbers 3
summaryBullets: This is the account of Aaron and Moses at the time the LORD spoke with Moses on Mount Sinai. (3:1).
These are the names of the sons of Aaron: Nadab the firstborn, then Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar. (3:2).
These were Aaron’s sons, the anointed priests, who were ordained to serve as priests. (3:3).

Nadab and Abihu, however, died in the presence of the LORD when they offered unauthorized fire before the LORD in the Wilderness of Sinai. And since they had no sons, only Eleazar and Ithamar served as priests during the lifetime of their father Aaron. (3:4).
Then the LORD said to Moses, (3:5).
“Bring the tribe of Levi and present them to Aaron the priest to assist him. (3:6).
They are to perform duties for him and for the whole congregation before the Tent of Meeting, attending to the service of the tabernacle. (3:7).
They shall take care of all the furnishings of the Tent of Meeting and fulfill obligations for the Israelites by attending to the service of the tabernacle. (3:8).
Assign the Levites to Aaron and his sons; they have been given exclusively to him from among the Israelites. (3:9).
So you shall appoint Aaron and his sons to carry out the duties of the priesthood; but any outsider who approaches the tabernacle must be put to death.” (3:10).
Again the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, (3:11).
“Behold, I have taken the Levites from among the children of Israel in place of every firstborn Israelite from the womb. The Levites belong to Me, (3:12).

for all the firstborn are Mine. On the day I struck down every firstborn in the land of Egypt, I consecrated to Myself all the firstborn in Israel, both man and beast. They are Mine; I am the LORD.” (3:13).
Then the LORD spoke to Moses in the Wilderness of Sinai, saying, (3:14).
“Number the Levites by their families and clans. You are to count every male a month old or more.” (3:15).
So Moses numbered them according to the word of the LORD, as he had been commanded. (3:16).
These were the sons of Levi by name: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. (3:17).
These were the names of the sons of Gershon by their clans: Libni and Shimei. (3:18).
The sons of Kohath by their clans were Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel. (3:19).
And the sons of Merari by their clans were Mahli and Mushi. These were the clans of the Levites, according to their families. (3:20).
From Gershon came the Libnite clan and the Shimeite clan; these were the Gershonite clans. (3:21).
The number of all the males a month old or more was 7,500. (3:22).
The Gershonite clans were to camp on the west, behind the tabernacle, (3:23).
and the leader of the families of the Gershonites was Eliasaph son of Lael. (3:24).

Then the LORD said to Moses, “Number every firstborn male of the Israelites a month old or more, and list their names. (3:40).
You are to take the Levites for Me— I am the LORD— in place of all the firstborn of Israel, and the livestock of the Levites in place of all the firstborn of the livestock of the Israelites.” (3:41).

“Take the Levites in place of all the firstborn of Israel, and the livestock of the Levites in place of their livestock. The Levites belong to Me; I am the LORD. (3:45).
To redeem the 273 firstborn Israelites who outnumber the Levites, (3:46).
you are to collect five shekels for each one, according to the sanctuary shekel of twenty gerahs. (3:47).
Give the money to Aaron and his sons as the redemption price for the excess among the Israelites.” (3:48).
So Moses collected the redemption money from those in excess of the number redeemed by the Levites. (3:49).
He collected the money from the firstborn of the Israelites: 1,365 shekels, according to the sanctuary shekel. (3:50).
And Moses gave the redemption money to Aaron and his sons in obedience to the word of the LORD, just as the LORD had commanded him. (3:51).

Exodus 13:1-2,11-15: Every firstborn male is set apart to the LORD because of the night Egypt lost its firstborn.
Exodus 12:29-30: At midnight the LORD strikes down every firstborn in the land of Egypt.

Exodus 30:13: A shekel of the sanctuary is twenty gerahs, and the half shekel is the census payment.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֵשׁ זָרָה (esh zarah), strange fire
translationNotes.note: The Hebrew says strange or foreign fire. Coals for the incense were to be taken from the altar itself (Leviticus 16:12), so bringing fire from anywhere else broke the one rule that governed the whole procedure. Leviticus 10:9 immediately follows with a ban on priests drinking wine before entering the tent, which the text places directly after the incident.

A weight, not a coin, since coinage did not exist yet: about 11.4 grams of silver, roughly two fifths of an ounce. Israel's official standard is confirmed by a stone weight found in Jerusalem inscribed beka, the half shekel, which weighs 5.71 grams. Payment was made by weighing metal on a balance, which is why honest weights are a recurring command (Leviticus 19:36).

The smallest weight in the Hebrew system, twenty to the shekel (Exodus 30:13), which puts it at about 0.57 grams, roughly the weight of a grain of barley. It exists because silver was cut and weighed for small transactions, and Ezekiel 45:12 uses it in the same reckoning. Five shekels is therefore a hundred gerahs of silver.

273 firstborn Israelites outnumbered the Levites, and each was redeemed at five shekels, giving the 1,365 shekels of verse 50, or about 15.6 kilograms of silver. For scale, a Levite hired as a household priest in Judges 17:10 was paid ten shekels of silver a year plus his clothes and food, so five shekels was about half a year's cash wage for a working man.

The Levite count starts at one month, not twenty, because it is not a muster. Infant mortality was high, and a month was the point at which a child was reckoned viable; the same threshold governs the redemption of the firstborn at 18:16 and the valuation lists of Leviticus 27:6. That is why 22,000 Levites can stand in for the firstborn of a nation of 603,550 fighting men without contradiction: the two counts measure different things.

stories.keyTakeaway: Aaron's sons Nadab and Abihu died when they offered unauthorized fire before the LORD; Eleazar and Ithamar remained as priests. The LORD assigns the Levites to assist Aaron and the priests, organizing them into three clans - Gershon, Kohath, and Merari - with specific duties and camp locations; when the Levites total 22,000 and the firstborn Israelites total 22,273, Moses collects redemption money for the 273 excess firstborn.

stories.title: 📊 Numbers 4
summaryBullets: Then the LORD said to Moses and Aaron, (4:1).
“Take a census of the Kohathites among the Levites by their clans and families, (4:2).
men from thirty to fifty years old— everyone who is qualified to serve in the work at the Tent of Meeting. (4:3).

And the LORD said to Moses, (4:21).

from thirty to fifty years old, counting everyone who comes to serve in the work at the Tent of Meeting. (4:23).

the curtains of the courtyard, and the curtains for the entrance at the gate of the courtyard that surrounds the tabernacle and altar, along with their ropes and all the equipment for their service. The Gershonites will do all that needs to be done with these items. (4:26).

This is the service of the Gershonite clans at the Tent of Meeting, and their duties shall be under the direction of Ithamar son of Aaron the priest. (4:28).
As for the sons of Merari, you are to number them by their clans and families, (4:29).
from thirty to fifty years old, counting everyone who comes to serve in the work of the Tent of Meeting. (4:30).

and the posts of the surrounding courtyard with their bases, tent pegs, and ropes, including all their equipment and everything related to their use. You shall assign by name the items that they are responsible to carry. (4:32).

So Moses, Aaron, and the leaders of the congregation numbered the Kohathites by their clans and families, (4:34).
everyone from thirty to fifty years old who came to serve in the work at the Tent of Meeting. (4:35).

These were counted from the Kohathite clans, everyone who could serve at the Tent of Meeting. Moses and Aaron numbered them according to the command of the LORD through Moses. (4:37).
Then the Gershonites were numbered by their clans and families, (4:38).
everyone from thirty to fifty years old who came to serve in the work at the Tent of Meeting. (4:39).

These were counted from the Gershonite clans who served at the Tent of Meeting, whom Moses and Aaron counted at the LORD’s command. (4:41).
And the Merarites were numbered by their clans and families, (4:42).
everyone from thirty to fifty years old who came to serve in the work at the Tent of Meeting. (4:43).

These were counted from the Merarite clans, whom Moses and Aaron numbered at the LORD’s command through Moses. (4:45).
So Moses, Aaron, and the leaders of Israel numbered by their clans and families all the Levites (4:46).
from thirty to fifty years old who came to do the work of serving and carrying the Tent of Meeting. (4:47).
And the number of men was 8,580. (4:48).
At the LORD’s command through Moses they were numbered, and each one was assigned his work and burden, as the LORD had commanded Moses. (4:49).
crossRefs: Numbers 8:23-26: The Levites begin service at twenty-five and retire from the labour at fifty.
2 Samuel 6:6-7: Uzzah puts out his hand to steady the ark on the cart and dies beside it.
1 Chronicles 15:12-15: The Levites carry the ark on their shoulders with the poles, as Moses had commanded.
Exodus 25:10-15: The poles are set in the rings of the ark and are never to be taken out.
1 Chronicles 23:24-27: David lowers the age of Levitical service to twenty once the ark has a permanent home.

translationNotes.note: This is the age band for the porterage: taking the sanctuary down, carrying it and setting it up. Numbers 8:24-25 gives a different band, twenty-five to fifty, for entering the service generally, and 1 Chronicles 23:24-27 drops the entry age to twenty once the ark has stopped moving and there is nothing left to carry. The ages track the physical work, and the text says so.

The Kohathites get no carts (7:9) because the ark and the holy vessels travel on poles across men's shoulders. Egyptian reliefs show sacred barques carried in exactly this way. Ignoring the rule is what kills Uzzah in 2 Samuel 6:6-7, and David says so when he does it properly the second time: because we did not seek Him according to the ordinance (1 Chronicles 15:13).

The covering material named here has been rendered badger skin, porpoise hide, dolphin skin and fine leather at different times, because the word appears only in the tabernacle texts and one line of Ezekiel 16:10, where it is a sandal material. What is clear is its function: it is the weatherproof outer layer, put on last over everything else.

translationNotes.term: Must not go in and look
translationNotes.note: The priests wrap every object before the Kohathites come near, so the carriers handle covered bundles and never see what is inside. Verse 20 makes looking a capital matter, and 1 Samuel 6:19 records men of Beth-shemesh struck down for looking into the ark. The instruction is a work procedure with a fatal safety rule attached, which is how the chapter presents it.

The three clans field 2,750 Kohathites, 2,630 Gershonites and 3,200 Merarites, and those add to the total in verse 48. Set that beside the 22,000 Levite males of all ages in 3:39: fewer than four in ten Levite males were in the age band, which is what an age-restricted roll looks like.

stories.keyTakeaway: God instructs Moses and Aaron to count the Levites aged thirty to fifty and assign them specific duties: Kohathites carry the holy furnishings, Gershonites carry the tabernacle coverings and courtyard items, and Merarites carry the structural frames and posts. The census totals 2,750 Kohathites, 2,630 Gershonites, and 3,200 Merarites, for 8,580 men in service.

stories.title: ⚖️ Numbers 5
summaryBullets: Then the LORD said to Moses, (5:1).
“Command the Israelites to send away from the camp anyone with a skin disease, anyone who has a bodily discharge, and anyone who is defiled by a dead body. (5:2).
You must send away male and female alike; send them outside the camp so they will not defile their camp, where I dwell among them.” (5:3).
So the Israelites did this, sending such people outside the camp. They did just as the LORD had instructed Moses. (5:4).
And the LORD said to Moses, (5:5).
“Tell the Israelites that when a man or woman acts unfaithfully against the LORD by committing any sin against another, that person is guilty (5:6).
and must confess the sin he has committed. He must make full restitution, add a fifth to its value, and give all this to the one he has wronged. (5:7).

But if the man has no relative to whom restitution can be made for the wrong, the restitution belongs to the LORD and must be given to the priest along with the ram of atonement, by which the atonement is made for him. (5:8).
Every sacred contribution the Israelites bring to the priest shall belong to him. (5:9).
Each man’s sacred gifts are his own, but whatever he gives to the priest will belong to the priest.” (5:10).
Then the LORD said to Moses, (5:11).
“Speak to the Israelites and tell them that if any man’s wife goes astray and is unfaithful to him (5:12).
by sleeping with another man, and it is concealed from her husband and her impurity is undetected (since there is no witness against her and she was not caught in the act), (5:13).

and if a feeling of jealousy comes over her husband and he suspects his wife who has defiled herself— or if a feeling of jealousy comes over him and he suspects her even though she has not defiled herself— (5:14).

then he is to bring his wife to the priest. He must also bring for her an offering of a tenth of an ephah of barley flour. He is not to pour oil over it or put frankincense on it, because it is a grain offering for jealousy, an offering of memorial as a reminder of iniquity. (5:15).
The priest is to bring the wife forward and have her stand before the LORD. (5:16).
Then he is to take some holy water in a clay jar and put some of the dust from the tabernacle floor into the water. (5:17).

After the priest has the woman stand before the LORD, he is to let down her hair and place in her hands the grain offering of memorial, which is the grain offering for jealousy. The priest is to hold the bitter water that brings a curse. (5:18).

And he is to put the woman under oath and say to her, ‘If no other man has slept with you and you have not gone astray and become defiled while under your husband’s authority, may you be immune to this bitter water that brings a curse. (5:19).
But if you have gone astray while under your husband’s authority and have defiled yourself and lain carnally with a man other than your husband’— (5:20).
and the priest shall have the woman swear under the oath of the curse— ‘then may the LORD make you an attested curse among your people by making your thigh shrivel and your belly swell. (5:21).
May this water that brings a curse enter your stomach and cause your belly to swell and your thigh to shrivel.’ Then the woman is to say, ‘Amen, Amen.’ (5:22).
And the priest shall write these curses on a scroll and wash them off into the bitter water. (5:23).
He is to have the woman drink the bitter water that brings a curse, and it will enter her and may cause her bitter suffering. (5:24).
The priest shall take from her hand the grain offering for jealousy, wave it before the LORD, and bring it to the altar. (5:25).
Then the priest is to take a handful of the grain offering as a memorial portion and burn it on the altar; after that he is to have the woman drink the water. (5:26).

When he has made her drink the water, if she has defiled herself and been unfaithful to her husband, then the water that brings a curse will enter her and cause bitter suffering; her belly will swell, her thigh will shrivel, and she will become accursed among her people. (5:27).
But if the woman has not defiled herself and is clean, she will be unaffected and able to conceive children. (5:28).
This is the law of jealousy when a wife goes astray and defiles herself while under her husband’s authority, (5:29).
or when a feeling of jealousy comes over a husband and he suspects his wife. He is to have the woman stand before the LORD, and the priest is to apply to her this entire law. (5:30).
The husband will be free from guilt, but the woman shall bear her iniquity.” (5:31).
crossRefs: Leviticus 13:45-46: The person with the infectious skin disease lives alone, outside the camp, as long as it lasts.
Leviticus 6:1-5: Full restitution plus a fifth for property obtained by deceit, paid on the day of the guilt offering.
Leviticus 20:10: Both the man and the woman taken in adultery are to be put to death.
Deuteronomy 19:15: One witness is not enough; a charge is established by two or three witnesses.
John 8:3-11: A woman caught in adultery is brought for judgment, and her accusers leave one by one.

translationNotes.note: Restitution for a wrong done by deceit is the full value of the item plus twenty percent, paid to the victim and not to the sanctuary. If the victim has died with no kinsman to receive it, it goes to the priest (5:8). Zacchaeus goes far past this standard when he promises fourfold (Luke 19:8), which is the penalty for a stolen and slaughtered sheep at Exodus 22:1.

Every other grain offering in the law is wheat flour, and this one is barley, the cheaper grain that was mostly animal feed and the food of the poor. It also comes without oil and without frankincense, the two things that made an offering fragrant and costly. The offering is deliberately stripped down, matching the sin offering of the very poor in Leviticus 5:11.

A married woman's hair was bound and covered in public, so unbinding it before the assembly was itself an exposure. The same verb is used of the man with a skin disease, whose hair must hang loose as a public sign (Leviticus 13:45). This is a formal disgracing, done before any verdict, and the text presents it as part of the procedure.

translationNotes.term: The bitter water that brings a curse
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מֵי הַמָּרִים הַמְאָרֲרִים (mei ha-marim ha-me'ararim)
translationNotes.note: Holy water in a clay jar, with dust from the tabernacle floor stirred in, and the written curses washed off the scroll into it so that the woman drinks the words themselves. This is the only trial by ordeal in the whole law, and it stands against a much harsher regional practice: the Babylonian laws of Hammurabi require a woman accused this way to throw herself into the river, where the current decides. Here nothing in the cup can hurt her, and the case turns entirely on the oath.

Exclusion here is not punishment and has nothing to do with morals. Skin disease, bodily discharge and contact with a corpse all made a person ritually unclean, and the camp had God's tent at its centre. Exclusion was temporary and ended with the prescribed washing. Chapter 19 supplies the procedure for the third of these three causes.

stories.keyTakeaway: The Israelites remove those with skin diseases and discharges from camp; God establishes restitution rules for wrongs committed and describes a ritual in which a priest administers bitter water to a wife suspected of adultery, with physical consequences following if she is guilty.

stories.title: ⚖️ Numbers 6
summaryBullets: And the LORD said to Moses, (6:1).
“Speak to the Israelites and tell them that if a man or woman makes a special vow, the vow of a Nazirite, to separate himself to the LORD, (6:2).
he is to abstain from wine and strong drink. He must not drink vinegar made from wine or strong drink, and he must not drink any grape juice or eat fresh grapes or raisins. (6:3).
All the days of his separation, he is not to eat anything that comes from the grapevine, not even the seeds or skins. (6:4).

For the entire period of his vow of separation, no razor shall touch his head. He must be holy until the time of his separation to the LORD is complete; he must let the hair of his head grow long. (6:5).
Throughout the days of his separation to the LORD, he must not go near a dead body. (6:6).
Even if his father or mother or brother or sister should die, he is not to defile himself, because the symbol of consecration to his God is upon his head. (6:7).
Throughout the time of his separation, he is holy to the LORD. (6:8).
If someone suddenly dies in his presence and defiles his consecrated head of hair, he must shave his head on the day of his cleansing — the seventh day. (6:9).
On the eighth day he must bring two turtledoves or two young pigeons to the priest at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting. (6:10).

And the priest is to offer one as a sin offering and the other as a burnt offering to make atonement for him, because he has sinned by being in the presence of the dead body. On that day he must consecrate his head again. (6:11).
He must rededicate his time of separation to the LORD and bring a year-old male lamb as a guilt offering. But the preceding days shall not be counted, because his separation was defiled. (6:12).
Now this is the law of the Nazirite when his time of separation is complete: He must be brought to the entrance to the Tent of Meeting, (6:13).

and he is to present an offering to the LORD of an unblemished year-old male lamb as a burnt offering, an unblemished year-old female lamb as a sin offering, and an unblemished ram as a peace offering — (6:14).
together with their grain offerings and drink offerings — and a basket of unleavened cakes made from fine flour mixed with oil and unleavened wafers coated with oil. (6:15).
The priest is to present all these before the LORD and make the sin offering and the burnt offering. (6:16).
He shall also offer the ram as a peace offering to the LORD, along with the basket of unleavened bread. And the priest is to offer the accompanying grain offering and drink offering. (6:17).
Then at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting, the Nazirite is to shave his consecrated head, take the hair, and put it on the fire under the peace offering. (6:18).

And the priest is to take the boiled shoulder from the ram, one unleavened cake from the basket, and one unleavened wafer, and put them into the hands of the Nazirite who has just shaved the hair of his consecration. (6:19).

The priest shall then wave them as a wave offering before the LORD. This is a holy portion for the priest, in addition to the breast of the wave offering and the thigh that was presented. After that, the Nazirite may drink wine. (6:20).

This is the law of the Nazirite who vows his offering to the LORD for his separation, in addition to whatever else he can afford; he must fulfill whatever vow he makes, according to the law of his separation.” (6:21).
Then the LORD said to Moses, (6:22).
“Tell Aaron and his sons:This is how you are to bless the Israelites. Say to them: (6:23).
‘May the LORD bless you and keep you; (6:24).
may the LORD cause His face to shine upon you and be gracious to you; (6:25).
may the LORD lift up His countenance toward you and give you peace.’ (6:26).
So they shall put My name on the Israelites, and I will bless them.” (6:27).
crossRefs: Judges 13:2-7: Samson is to be a Nazirite to God from the womb, and no razor is ever to touch his head.
1 Samuel 1:11: Hannah vows that if she is given a son, no razor will come upon his head all his life.
Amos 2:11-12: I raised up Nazirites from among your sons, but you made the Nazirites drink wine.
Acts 21:23-26: Four men are under a vow, and Paul pays the cost of their purification and their shaving.
Psalm 67:1: May God be gracious to us and bless us and make His face shine upon us.

translationNotes.note: From a root meaning to separate or set apart. It is not a priesthood and not a lifelong caste: any man or woman could take it, for a stated period, and then end it. The three abstentions are precise: nothing from the grapevine at all, including skins and seeds (6:3-4), no razor on the head (6:5), and no going near a dead body even for a parent (6:6-7). Samson and Samuel were placed under it from birth by others, which is the exception rather than the pattern.

translationNotes.term: Anything that comes from the grapevine
translationNotes.note: The ban goes far beyond wine. Vinegar, grape juice, fresh grapes, raisins, skins and seeds are all named. Wine was the ordinary table drink because water was often unsafe, and raisins were preserved food, so this cut the Nazirite out of normal meals and normal hospitality. That is what the separation was visibly for.

The uncut hair itself is called a nezer, the same word used for the golden plate on the high priest's turban and for a royal crown (Exodus 29:6; 2 Kings 11:12). At the end of the vow the hair is shaved off at the tent entrance and burned in the fire under the peace offering (6:18), so the crown is destroyed on the altar rather than kept.

translationNotes.term: If someone suddenly dies in his presence
translationNotes.note: A death nearby with no warning voids the whole term. He shaves on the seventh day, brings two turtledoves or two young pigeons on the eighth, and starts the count again from zero; the days already served do not carry over (6:9-12). Turtledoves and pigeons were the offering of a person who could not afford a lamb (Leviticus 5:7), so the law makes the restart affordable.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יְבָרֶכְךָ יְהוָה וְיִשְׁמְרֶךָ (yevarekhekha YHWH ve-yishmerekha)
translationNotes.note: The oldest known text of any part of the Bible is this blessing. In 1979 Gabriel Barkay excavated a burial cave at Ketef Hinnom just outside Jerusalem and found two tiny rolled silver plaques, dated to the late seventh or early sixth century BC, inscribed with words matching Numbers 6:24-26. They were worn as amulets, which means this blessing was already being carried on a person's body before the exile.

stories.keyTakeaway: God instructs Moses on the Nazirite vow - a dedication requiring abstinence from wine and grapes, uncut hair, and avoidance of the dead - with prescribed offerings and procedures for completion and cleansing. God also commands Aaron and his sons to bless the Israelites with a specific formula invoking the Lord's blessing, favor, and peace.

summaryBullets: On the day Moses finished setting up the tabernacle, he anointed and consecrated it and all its furnishings, along with the altar and all its utensils. (7:1).
And the leaders of Israel, the heads of their families, presented an offering. These men were the tribal leaders who had supervised the registration. (7:2).
They brought as their offering before the LORD six covered carts and twelve oxen — an ox from each leader and a cart from every two leaders — and presented them before the tabernacle. (7:3).
And the LORD said to Moses, (7:4).
“Accept these gifts from them, that they may be used in the work of the Tent of Meeting. And give them to the Levites, to each man according to his service.” (7:5).
So Moses took the carts and oxen and gave them to the Levites. (7:6).
He gave the Gershonites two carts and four oxen, as their service required, (7:7).
and he gave the Merarites four carts and eight oxen, as their service required, all under the direction of Ithamar son of Aaron the priest. (7:8).
But he did not give any to the Kohathites, since they were to carry on their shoulders the holy objects for which they were responsible. (7:9).
When the altar was anointed, the leaders approached with their offerings for its dedication and presented them before the altar. (7:10).
And the LORD said to Moses, “Each day one leader is to present his offering for the dedication of the altar.” (7:11).
On the first day Nahshon son of Amminadab from the tribe of Judah drew near with his offering. (7:12).

His offering was one silver platter weighing a hundred and thirty shekels, and one silver bowl weighing seventy shekels, both according to the sanctuary shekel and filled with fine flour mixed with oil for a grain offering; (7:13).

crossRefs: Exodus 40:17-33: Moses raises the tabernacle on the first day of the first month of the second year.
Exodus 25:22: I will meet with you there and speak to you from above the mercy seat, between the two cherubim.
Numbers 4:15: The Kohathites carry the holy things but must not touch them, or they will die.
2 Samuel 6:3-7: The ark set on a new cart, and Uzzah struck down when the oxen stumble.

translationNotes.note: At about 11.4 grams to the sanctuary shekel, that platter weighs close to 1.5 kilograms of silver and the bowl of 70 shekels about 800 grams. Each of the twelve leaders brings the identical pair, so verse 85 totals 2,400 shekels, about 27 kilograms, which is four fifths of a talent. The twelve gold dishes of ten shekels each come to 120 shekels, about 1.4 kilograms of gold.

The largest weight in the system, 3,000 shekels, about 34 kilograms or 75 pounds. It is a unit of weight and of money, not an ability; the English sense of a natural gift comes from the parable in Matthew 25 and is a much later development. A talent of silver was more than most families would see in a lifetime.

translationNotes.term: Six covered carts and twelve oxen
translationNotes.note: Two-wheeled ox carts, given to the Gershonites and Merarites who hauled the heavy curtains, frames, bars and sockets. The Kohathites got none, because their load went on the shoulder. The distinction is exactly what David gets wrong centuries later, moving the ark on a cart and losing a man for it (2 Samuel 6:3-7), before correcting it (1 Chronicles 15:15).

The chapter runs to eighty-nine verses because it writes out the identical offering twelve separate times, once per tribe, instead of listing it once and saying the others matched. Ancient legal and dedicatory records were kept that way on purpose, so that each party's contribution stood on the record in its own right. It is the longest chapter in the book and the second longest in the Bible.

Two figures of hammered gold facing each other across the lid of the ark, wings spread forward (Exodus 25:18-20). Winged guardian figures flanking a throne are known across the ancient Near East, and carved ivory examples have been found at Megiddo and Nimrud. The last verse of this chapter says the voice came from that space between them, which is where Exodus 25:22 said it would.

stories.keyTakeaway: Moses consecrates the tabernacle and altar; tribal leaders donate carts and oxen to the Levites, then each of the twelve tribal leaders presents an identical dedication offering over twelve days. When Moses enters the tent of meeting, he hears the LORD speaking from between the cherubim above the atonement cover.

stories.title: ⚖️ Numbers 8
summaryBullets: Then the LORD said to Moses, (8:1).
“Speak to Aaron and tell him: ‘When you set up the seven lamps, they are to light the area in front of the lampstand.’” (8:2).
And Aaron did so; he set up the lamps facing toward the front of the lampstand, just as the LORD had commanded Moses. (8:3).
This is how the lampstand was constructed: it was made of hammered gold from its base to its blossoms, fashioned according to the pattern the LORD had shown Moses. (8:4).
Again the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, (8:5).
“Take the Levites from among the Israelites and make them ceremonially clean. (8:6).
This is what you must do to cleanse them: Sprinkle them with the water of purification. Have them shave their whole bodies and wash their clothes, and so purify themselves. (8:7).
Then have them take a young bull with its grain offering of fine flour mixed with oil, and you are to take a second young bull for a sin offering. (8:8).
Bring the Levites before the Tent of Meeting and assemble the whole congregation of Israel. (8:9).
You are to present the Levites before the LORD and have the Israelites lay their hands upon them. (8:10).
Aaron is to present the Levites before the LORD as a wave offering from the sons of Israel, so that they may perform the service of the LORD. (8:11).
And the Levites are to lay their hands on the heads of the bulls, and offer to the LORD one as a sin offering and the other as a burnt offering, to make atonement for the Levites. (8:12).
You are to have the Levites stand before Aaron and his sons and then present them before the LORD as a wave offering. (8:13).
In this way you shall separate the Levites from the rest of the Israelites, and the Levites will belong to Me. (8:14).
After you have cleansed them and presented them as a wave offering, they may come to serve at the Tent of Meeting. (8:15).
For the Levites have been wholly given to Me from among the sons of Israel. I have taken them for Myself in place of all who come first from the womb, the firstborn of all the sons of Israel. (8:16).
For every firstborn male in Israel is Mine, both man and beast. I set them apart for Myself on the day I struck down all the firstborn in the land of Egypt. (8:17).
But I have taken the Levites in place of all the firstborn among the sons of Israel. (8:18).

And I have given the Levites as a gift to Aaron and his sons from among the Israelites, to perform the service for the Israelites at the Tent of Meeting and to make atonement on their behalf, so that no plague will come against the Israelites when they approach the sanctuary.” (8:19).
So Moses, Aaron, and the whole congregation of Israel did with the Levites everything that the LORD had commanded Moses they should do. (8:20).
The Levites purified themselves and washed their clothes, and Aaron presented them as a wave offering before the LORD. Aaron also made atonement for them to cleanse them. (8:21).
After that, the Levites came to perform their service at the Tent of Meeting in the presence of Aaron and his sons. Thus they did with the Levites just as the LORD had commanded Moses. (8:22).
And the LORD said to Moses, (8:23).
“This applies to the Levites: Men twenty-five years of age or older shall enter to perform the service in the work at the Tent of Meeting. (8:24).
But at the age of fifty, they must retire from performing the work and no longer serve. (8:25).

After that, they may assist their brothers in fulfilling their duties at the Tent of Meeting, but they themselves are not to do the work. This is how you are to assign responsibilities to the Levites.” (8:26).
crossRefs: Exodus 25:31-40: The lampstand hammered from one piece of pure gold, with cups shaped like almond blossoms.
Leviticus 24:1-4: Aaron tends the lamps before the LORD continually, from evening until morning.
Numbers 4:3: The census of Levites for the carrying duty counts only men from thirty to fifty.
Numbers 3:12-13: The Levites taken by God in place of every firstborn son among the Israelites.
Ezra 3:8: Levites twenty years old and upward appointed to supervise the rebuilding of the house of the LORD.

translationNotes.note: A single piece of hammered gold with a central shaft and six branches, holding seven lamps that burned olive oil (Exodus 25:31-40). It stood inside the tent, not in daylight, and was the only light in that room. A seven-branched lampstand carried off from the temple in Jerusalem in AD 70 is carved on the Arch of Titus in Rome, which is the earliest surviving picture of one.

Literally water of sin offering, and not the same thing as the water of separation made from the red heifer's ashes in chapter 19, which English versions also render water of purification. Here it comes with shaving the whole body and washing the clothes, the same full-body procedure the Greek historian Herodotus records of Egyptian priests in the fifth century BC. It is done once, at the start, to put the whole tribe into service.

The gesture of lifting an offering and moving it forward and back before the altar, marking it as handed over to God and then handed back for use. What makes this passage unusual is that the offering being waved is people: Aaron presents the whole tribe of Levi with that motion (8:11,21). The Israelites first lay their hands on the Levites, the same act a worshipper performs on an animal.

This chapter sets entry at twenty-five and retirement from the labour at fifty; chapter 4 sets the porterage band at thirty to fifty. The simplest reading of the two together is a five-year apprenticeship before the heavy work. Retirement is not total: verse 26 says the older men may still stand guard duty with their brothers, but must not do the work itself.

stories.keyTakeaway: Aaron sets up the lamps on the lampstand to light the area in front of it as commanded. Moses purifies the Levites through ritual cleansing and presents them as a wave offering to the LORD, dedicating them to serve at the tent of meeting in place of Israel's firstborn; their service begins at age twenty-five and ends at fifty.

stories.title: ⚖️ Numbers 9
summaryBullets: In the first month of the second year after Israel had come out of the land of Egypt, the LORD spoke to Moses in the Wilderness of Sinai: (9:1).
“The Israelites are to observe the Passover at its appointed time. (9:2).
You are to observe it at the appointed time, at twilight on the fourteenth day of this month, in accordance with its statutes and ordinances.” (9:3).
So Moses told the Israelites to observe the Passover, (9:4).
and they did so in the Wilderness of Sinai, at twilight on the fourteenth day of the first month. The Israelites did everything just as the LORD had commanded Moses. (9:5).
But there were some men who were unclean due to a dead body, so they could not observe the Passover on that day. And they came before Moses and Aaron that same day (9:6).
and said to Moses, “We are unclean because of a dead body, but why should we be excluded from presenting the LORD’s offering with the other Israelites at the appointed time?” (9:7).
“Wait here until I find out what the LORD commands concerning you,” Moses replied. (9:8).
Then the LORD said to Moses, (9:9).
“Tell the Israelites: ‘When any one of you or your descendants is unclean because of a dead body, or is away on a journey, he may still observe the Passover to the LORD. (9:10).
Such people are to observe it at twilight on the fourteenth day of the second month. They are to eat the lamb, together with unleavened bread and bitter herbs; (9:11).
they may not leave any of it until morning or break any of its bones. They must observe the Passover according to all its statutes. (9:12).

But if a man who is ceremonially clean and is not on a journey still fails to observe the Passover, he must be cut off from his people, because he did not present the LORD’s offering at its appointed time. That man will bear the consequences of his sin. (9:13).

If a foreigner dwelling among you wants to observe the Passover to the LORD, he is to do so according to the Passover statute and its ordinances. You are to apply the same statute to both the foreigner and the native of the land.’” (9:14).
On the day that the tabernacle, the Tent of the Testimony, was set up, the cloud covered it and appeared like fire above the tabernacle from evening until morning. (9:15).
It remained that way continually; the cloud would cover the tabernacle by day, and at night it would appear like fire. (9:16).
Whenever the cloud was lifted from above the Tent, the Israelites would set out, and wherever the cloud settled, there the Israelites would camp. (9:17).
At the LORD’s command the Israelites set out, and at the LORD’s command they camped. As long as the cloud remained over the tabernacle, they remained encamped. (9:18).
Even when the cloud lingered over the tabernacle for many days, the Israelites kept the LORD’s charge and did not set out. (9:19).
Sometimes the cloud remained over the tabernacle for only a few days, and they would camp at the LORD’s command and set out at the LORD’s command. (9:20).

Sometimes the cloud remained only from evening until morning, and when it lifted in the morning, they would set out. Whether it was by day or by night, when the cloud was taken up, they would set out. (9:21).

Whether the cloud lingered for two days, a month, or longer, the Israelites camped and did not set out as long as the cloud remained over the tabernacle; but when it was lifted, they would set out. (9:22).
They camped at the LORD’s command, and they set out at the LORD’s command; they carried out the LORD’s charge according to His command through Moses. (9:23).
crossRefs: Exodus 12:1-13: The first Passover, the lamb taken on the tenth day and killed at twilight on the fourteenth.
Exodus 12:46: It must be eaten in one house, and you shall not break any of its bones.
2 Chronicles 30:1-3,15: Hezekiah keeps the Passover in the second month, since the priests were not consecrated in time.
Exodus 40:34-38: The cloud covers the tent and the glory fills the tabernacle, and there is fire in it by night.
John 19:36: These things happened so that the Scripture would be fulfilled: not one of His bones will be broken.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בֵּין הָעַרְבַּיִם (bein ha-'arbayim), between the two evenings
translationNotes.note: The Hebrew phrase means between the two evenings, and its exact window was disputed within Israel itself. The Samaritans and, later, the Karaites took it as the gap between sunset and full dark; the Pharisees took it as the afternoon from the sun's decline to sunset, which is why the temple lambs were killed in mid-afternoon. The same phrase fixes the evening lamb of the daily offering (Exodus 29:39).

A make-up date exactly one month later, the fourteenth day of the second month, for anyone who was unclean through contact with a corpse or away on a journey (9:10-11). It is the only appointed time in the law with a second chance built into it, and it exists because men brought a real case to Moses in verses 6 to 8. Hezekiah invokes it for a whole nation in 2 Chronicles 30.

The signal system for a nation on the move: while it settled, they stayed, and when it lifted, they packed. Verses 19 to 22 make the point that the stops had no pattern a person could predict, one night or a month or a year, so the camp could never plan the next move for itself. That is the whole administrative fact this chapter is recording.

The karet penalty, applied here to a clean man who is at home and still refuses to keep the Passover (9:13). The phrase covers exclusion from the community and, in some passages, being ended without descendants; the text never spells out a court procedure for it, which is one reason it stands apart from the penalties judges administer. It attaches to a short list of offences, including eating leaven in Passover week (Exodus 12:15).

stories.keyTakeaway: The Israelites celebrate Passover in the Desert of Sinai; those unclean from contact with a dead body or traveling are permitted to observe it a month later with the same regulations. The cloud above the tabernacle guides the people's movements - they camp when it settles and depart when it lifts, following the LORD's direction through these signs.

stories.title: ⚖️ Numbers 10
summaryBullets: Then the LORD said to Moses, (10:1).
“Make two trumpets of hammered silver to be used for calling the congregation and for having the camps set out. (10:2).
When both are sounded, the whole congregation is to assemble before you at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting. (10:3).
But if only one is sounded, then the leaders, the heads of the clans of Israel, are to gather before you. (10:4).
When you sound short blasts, the camps that lie on the east side are to set out. (10:5).
When you sound the short blasts a second time, the camps that lie on the south side are to set out. The blasts are to signal them to set out. (10:6).
To convene the assembly, you are to sound long blasts, not short ones. (10:7).
The sons of Aaron, the priests, are to sound the trumpets. This shall be a permanent statute for you and the generations to come. (10:8).

When you enter into battle in your land against an adversary who attacks you, sound short blasts on the trumpets, and you will be remembered before the LORD your God and saved from your enemies. (10:9).

And on your joyous occasions, your appointed feasts, and the beginning of each month, you are to blow the trumpets over your burnt offerings and peace offerings to serve as a reminder for you before your God. I am the LORD your God.” (10:10).
On the twentieth day of the second month of the second year, the cloud was lifted from above the tabernacle of the Testimony, (10:11).
and the Israelites set out from the Wilderness of Sinai, traveling from place to place until the cloud settled in the Wilderness of Paran. (10:12).
They set out this first time according to the LORD’s command through Moses. (10:13).
First, the divisions of the camp of Judah set out under their standard, with Nahshon son of Amminadab in command. (10:14).
Nethanel son of Zuar was over the division of the tribe of Issachar, (10:15).
and Eliab son of Helon was over the division of the tribe of Zebulun. (10:16).
Then the tabernacle was taken down, and the Gershonites and the Merarites set out, transporting it. (10:17).
Then the divisions of the camp of Reuben set out under their standard, with Elizur son of Shedeur in command. (10:18).
Shelumiel son of Zurishaddai was over the division of the tribe of Simeon, (10:19).
and Eliasaph son of Deuel was over the division of the tribe of Gad. (10:20).
Then the Kohathites set out, transporting the holy objects; the tabernacle was to be set up before their arrival. (10:21).
Next, the divisions of the camp of Ephraim set out under their standard, with Elishama son of Ammihud in command. (10:22).
Gamaliel son of Pedahzur was over the division of the tribe of Manasseh, (10:23).
and Abidan son of Gideoni was over the division of the tribe of Benjamin. (10:24).
Finally, the divisions of the camp of Dan set out under their standard, serving as the rear guard for all units, with Ahiezer son of Ammishaddai in command. (10:25).
Pagiel son of Ocran was over the division of the tribe of Asher, (10:26).
and Ahira son of Enan was over the division of the tribe of Naphtali. (10:27).
This was the order of march for the Israelite divisions as they set out. (10:28).

Then Moses said to Hobab, the son of Moses’ father-in-law Reuel the Midianite, “We are setting out for the place of which the LORD said: ‘I will give it to you.’ Come with us, and we will treat you well, for the LORD has promised good things to Israel.” (10:29).
“I will not go,” Hobab replied. “Instead, I am going back to my own land and my own people.” (10:30).
“Please do not leave us,” Moses said, “since you know where we should camp in the wilderness, and you can serve as our eyes. (10:31).
If you come with us, we will share with you whatever good things the LORD gives us.” (10:32).
So they set out on a three-day journey from the mountain of the LORD, with the ark of the covenant of the LORD traveling ahead of them for those three days to seek a resting place for them. (10:33).
And the cloud of the LORD was over them by day when they set out from the camp. (10:34).
Whenever the ark set out, Moses would say, “Rise up, O LORD! May Your enemies be scattered; may those who hate You flee before You.” (10:35).
And when it came to rest, he would say: “Return, O LORD, to the countless thousands of Israel.” (10:36).
crossRefs: 2 Chronicles 13:12-15: The priests sound the trumpets for battle, and the men of Judah raise the war cry.
Joshua 6:4-5: Seven priests carry seven rams' horns before the ark and blow them at Jericho.
Psalm 68:1: Let God arise, let His enemies be scattered, the words Moses says whenever the ark set out.
Exodus 18:1-12: Jethro, priest of Midian and father-in-law to Moses, comes to the camp at the mountain of God.
1 Corinthians 14:8: If the trumpet does not give a distinct call, who will get ready for battle?

translationNotes.note: These are not rams' horns. A chatsotserah is a manufactured instrument, a long straight tube of beaten silver with a flared bell, and only the priests were allowed to blow them (10:8). Two such trumpets, carried off from Jerusalem in AD 70, are carved beside the lampstand on the Arch of Titus in Rome. The ram's horn, the shofar, is a different instrument used by anybody.

The system has exactly two calls and the text distinguishes them carefully. A sustained blast on both trumpets means the whole congregation assembles at the tent entrance; on one trumpet only, it summons the tribal leaders (10:3-4). A teru'ah, a broken staccato blast, means break camp and move out, east side first, then south (10:5-6). Verse 7 states the rule that keeps them apart: to convene the assembly you blow long, not staccato.

The distance travelled from Sinai before the first stop, with the ark going ahead to scout a camping place (10:33). Deuteronomy 1:2 gives the other end of this leg: eleven days on foot from Horeb by the Mount Seir road to Kadesh-barnea. Those two figures are the only travel times the wilderness narrative supplies, and they describe a march of weeks, not the forty years that followed the refusal in chapter 14.

Midian descends from Abraham by Keturah (Genesis 25:1-2) and its people ranged the desert margins of northwest Arabia and Transjordan. Moses married into them and his father-in-law was a priest of Midian (Exodus 2:16-21; 3:1). Moses asks Hobab to stay because he knows the water and the campsites, which is the practical expertise of a desert people. Twenty-one chapters later Israel goes to war with Midian, and the reason is given at 31:16.

The two short sayings in verses 35 and 36 are a marching formula, spoken every time the ark went out and every time it stopped. Psalm 68:1 opens by quoting the first of them, and 2 Chronicles 6:41 draws on the second at the dedication of the temple. In the Hebrew manuscripts these two verses are set off by inverted marks, an ancient scribal notation, which shows they were treated as a distinct unit very early.

stories.keyTakeaway: God instructs Moses to make two silver trumpets for assembling the community and signaling the camps to set out, with Aaron's sons to blow them; the Israelites depart from Sinai in formation with Judah leading, the tabernacle following in the middle, and Dan bringing up the rear, while Moses invites his father-in-law Hobab to join them as a guide.

stories.title: 😠 Numbers 11
summaryBullets: Soon the people began to complain about their hardship in the hearing of the LORD, and when He heard them, His anger was kindled, and fire from the LORD blazed among them and consumed the outskirts of the camp. (11:1).
And the people cried out to Moses, and he prayed to the LORD, and the fire died down. (11:2).
So that place was called Taberah, because the fire of the LORD had burned among them. (11:3).
Meanwhile, the rabble among them had a strong craving for other food, and again the Israelites wept and said, “Who will feed us meat? (11:4).
We remember the fish we ate freely in Egypt, along with the cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions, and garlic. (11:5).
But now our appetite is gone; there is nothing to see but this manna!” (11:6).
Now the manna resembled coriander seed, and its appearance was like that of gum resin. (11:7).

The people walked around and gathered it, ground it on a handmill or crushed it in a mortar, then boiled it in a cooking pot or shaped it into cakes. It tasted like pastry baked with fine oil. (11:8).
When the dew fell on the camp at night, the manna would fall with it. (11:9).
Then Moses heard the people of family after family weeping at the entrances to their tents, and the anger of the LORD was kindled greatly, and Moses was also displeased. (11:10).
So Moses asked the LORD, “Why have You brought this trouble on Your servant? Why have I not found favor in Your sight, that You have laid upon me the burden of all these people? (11:11).

Did I conceive all these people? Did I give them birth, so that You should tell me, ‘Carry them in your bosom, as a nurse carries an infant,’ to the land that You swore to give their fathers? (11:12).
Where can I get meat for all these people? For they keep crying out to me, ‘Give us meat to eat!’ (11:13).
I cannot carry all these people by myself; it is too burdensome for me. (11:14).
If this is how You are going to treat me, please kill me right now — if I have found favor in Your eyes — and let me not see my own wretchedness.” (11:15).

Then the LORD said to Moses, “Bring Me seventy of the elders of Israel known to you as leaders and officers of the people. Bring them to the Tent of Meeting and have them stand there with you. (11:16).

And I will come down and speak with you there, and I will take some of the Spirit that is on you and put that Spirit on them. They will help you bear the burden of the people, so that you do not have to bear it by yourself. (11:17).

And say to the people: Consecrate yourselves for tomorrow, and you will eat meat, because you have cried out in the hearing of the LORD, saying: ‘Who will feed us meat? For we were better off in Egypt!’ Therefore the LORD will give you meat, and you will eat. (11:18).
You will eat it not for one or two days, nor for five or ten or twenty days, (11:19).

but for a whole month— until it comes out of your nostrils and makes you nauseous— because you have rejected the LORD, who is among you, and have cried out before Him, saying, ‘Why did we ever leave Egypt?’” (11:20).
But Moses replied, “Here I am among 600,000 men on foot, yet You say, ‘I will give them meat, and they will eat for a month.’ (11:21).
If all our flocks and herds were slaughtered for them, would they have enough? Or if all the fish in the sea were caught for them, would they have enough?” (11:22).
The LORD answered Moses, “Is the LORD’s arm too short? Now you will see whether or not My word will come to pass.” (11:23).
So Moses went out and relayed to the people the words of the LORD, and he gathered seventy of the elders of the people and had them stand around the tent. (11:24).

Then the LORD came down in the cloud and spoke to him, and He took some of the Spirit that was on Moses and placed that Spirit on the seventy elders. As the Spirit rested on them, they prophesied — but they never did so again. (11:25).

Two men, however, had remained in the camp — one named Eldad and the other Medad — and the Spirit rested on them. They were among those listed, but they had not gone out to the tent, and they prophesied in the camp. (11:26).
A young man ran and reported to Moses, “Eldad and Medad are prophesying in the camp.” (11:27).
Joshua son of Nun, the attendant to Moses since youth, spoke up and said, “Moses, my lord, stop them!” (11:28).
But Moses replied, “Are you jealous on my account? I wish that all the LORD’s people were prophets and that the LORD would place His Spirit on them!” (11:29).
Then Moses returned to the camp, along with the elders of Israel. (11:30).

Now a wind sent by the LORD came up, drove in quail from the sea, and brought them near the camp, about two cubits above the surface of the ground, for a day’s journey in every direction around the camp. (11:31).
All that day and night, and all the next day, the people stayed up gathering the quail. No one gathered less than ten homers, and they spread them out all around the camp. (11:32).
But while the meat was still between their teeth, before it was chewed, the anger of the LORD burned against the people, and the LORD struck them with a severe plague. (11:33).
So they called that place Kibroth-hattaavah, because there they buried the people who had craved other food. (11:34).
From Kibroth-hattaavah the people moved on to Hazeroth, where they remained for some time. (11:35).
crossRefs: Exodus 16:2-15: Manna and quail first given in the Wilderness of Sin, a month out of Egypt.
Exodus 16:31: The manna was white like coriander seed and tasted like wafers made with honey.
Psalm 78:26-31: He rained meat on them like dust, and His anger rose while the food was still in their mouths.
Psalm 106:14-15: He gave them what they asked for, but sent a wasting disease among them.
Joel 2:28-29: I will pour out My Spirit on all flesh, and your sons and daughters will prophesy.

translationNotes.note: Fish, cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions and garlic (11:5) is an accurate list of the Egyptian working diet, all of it recorded in Egyptian sources and tomb paintings. Nile fish were so plentiful they were a staple of the poor, and onions and garlic were issued to labourers. The complaint is specific and it is homesickness for a real menu, not a vague grumble.

Described here as looking like coriander seed, a pale round seed about three millimetres across, with the appearance of bdellium, an aromatic gum resin. It was processed like grain: ground in a hand mill or pounded in a mortar, boiled or baked into cakes, and it tasted of cakes made with oil (11:8). Exodus 16:31 compares the taste to honey wafers. The people are not complaining that it was unpleasant; they are complaining that it was the only thing there was.

The common quail migrates in enormous flocks across the eastern Mediterranean and Sinai every spring and autumn, flying at night and coming down exhausted, where they can be taken by hand or netted in quantity. Egyptians harvested them commercially on the coast, a trade that continued into modern times. Verse 31 describes exactly that: a wind off the sea driving them in low around the camp.

A homer is the largest dry measure, ten ephahs, roughly 220 litres, and the word is related to chamor, a donkey, meaning a donkey load. Ten homers is therefore about 2,200 litres of birds gathered by the person who gathered least (11:32). It is a deliberately absurd quantity, which is the point of the sentence.

The name means graves of craving, and verse 34 says it was given because they buried there the people who had craved. Place names in Scripture regularly record what happened at them: Meribah is quarrelling (20:13), Taberah at the start of this chapter is burning (11:3), Massah is testing (Exodus 17:7). The map itself was kept as a record.

stories.keyTakeaway: The people complain about their food and crave meat instead of manna; Moses grows frustrated under the burden and God appoints seventy elders to share it, then sends quail that causes a plague when the people eat it.

stories.title: 😠 Numbers 12
summaryBullets: Then Miriam and Aaron criticized Moses because of the Cushite woman he had married, for he had taken a Cushite wife. (12:1).
“Does the LORD speak only through Moses?” they said. “Does He not also speak through us?” And the LORD heard this. (12:2).
Now Moses was a very humble man, more so than any man on the face of the earth. (12:3).
And suddenly the LORD said to Moses, Aaron, and Miriam, “You three, come out to the Tent of Meeting.” So the three went out, (12:4).
and the LORD came down in a pillar of cloud, stood at the entrance to the Tent, and summoned Aaron and Miriam. When both of them had stepped forward, (12:5).
He said, “Hear now My words: If there is a prophet among you, I, the LORD, will reveal Myself to him in a vision; I will speak to him in a dream. (12:6).
But this is not so with My servant Moses; he is faithful in all My house. (12:7).
I speak with him face to face, clearly and not in riddles; he sees the form of the LORD. Why then were you unafraid to speak against My servant Moses?” (12:8).
So the anger of the LORD burned against them, and He departed. (12:9).
As the cloud lifted from above the Tent, suddenly Miriam became leprous, white as snow. Aaron turned toward her, saw that she was leprous, (12:10).
and said to Moses, “My lord, please do not hold against us this sin we have so foolishly committed. (12:11).
Please do not let her be like a stillborn infant whose flesh is half consumed when he comes out of his mother’s womb.” (12:12).
So Moses cried out to the LORD, “O God, please heal her!” (12:13).

But the LORD answered Moses, “If her father had but spit in her face, would she not have been in disgrace for seven days? Let her be confined outside the camp for seven days; after that she may be brought back in.” (12:14).
So Miriam was confined outside the camp for seven days, and the people did not move on until she was brought in again. (12:15).
After that, the people set out from Hazeroth and camped in the Wilderness of Paran. (12:16).
crossRefs: Exodus 15:20-21: Miriam the prophetess takes a tambourine and leads the women in song after the sea.
Leviticus 13:45-46: The person with the infectious skin disease lives outside the camp with clothes torn and hair loose.
Deuteronomy 24:8-9: Remember what the LORD your God did to Miriam on the way as you came out of Egypt.
Deuteronomy 25:9: Spitting in the face before the elders as a formal act of public disgrace.
Hebrews 3:2-6: Moses was faithful in all God's house as a servant, quoting the words of Numbers 12:7.

translationNotes.note: Cush is the land south of Egypt along the upper Nile, covering modern Sudan and southern Egypt, called Nubia in ancient sources. Isaiah 18:1-2 describes its people, and Jeremiah 13:23 refers to the Cushite's skin. The text names the marriage as the pretext for the complaint and then says nothing more about it; verse 2 gives what the argument was actually about, which is authority.

Tsara'at is not the disease modern medicine calls leprosy, which is Hansen's disease. It is a category of surface conditions, and Leviticus 13 and 14 apply the same word to mould in a fabric and to a growth in the plaster of a house. It made a person ritually unclean rather than medically contagious, and the priest's job was to inspect and declare, not to treat.

The comparison in verse 14 is precise. Spitting in the face was a formal act of shaming with a fixed consequence: a widow whose brother-in-law refuses to marry her pulls off his sandal and spits in his face before the elders (Deuteronomy 25:9). The LORD's argument is that a father's public disgrace of his daughter would carry a seven-day exclusion, so this one does too.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: פֶּה אֶל-פֶּה (peh el-peh), mouth to mouth
translationNotes.note: The Hebrew says mouth to mouth, and the contrast in verses 6 to 8 is between two modes of speaking. To a prophet God makes Himself known in a vision or a dream and speaks in riddles; with Moses He speaks directly and plainly. Exodus 33:11 uses the parallel phrase, panim el panim, face to face, as a man speaks with his friend.

The word means bowed down or afflicted, and elsewhere it is translated poor, meek or lowly (Psalm 37:11; Isaiah 61:1). It describes a position rather than a personality: a man with no claim of his own to press, which is why the sentence sits here, in the middle of a dispute about rank that Moses does not answer for himself.

stories.keyTakeaway: Miriam and Aaron criticize Moses over his Cushite wife and question whether the Lord speaks only through him; the Lord rebukes them, strikes Miriam with leprosy, and after Moses intercedes she is healed and confined outside the camp for seven days.

headings.text: The Complaint of Miriam and Aaron

stories.title: 😠 Numbers 13
summaryBullets: And the LORD said to Moses, (13:1).
“Send out for yourself men to spy out the land of Canaan, which I am giving to the Israelites. From each of their fathers’ tribes send one man who is a leader among them.” (13:2).
So at the command of the LORD, Moses sent them out from the Wilderness of Paran. All the men were leaders of the Israelites, (13:3).
and these were their names: From the tribe of Reuben, Shammua son of Zaccur; (13:4).
from the tribe of Simeon, Shaphat son of Hori; (13:5).
from the tribe of Judah, Caleb son of Jephunneh; (13:6).
from the tribe of Issachar, Igal son of Joseph; (13:7).
from the tribe of Ephraim, Hoshea son of Nun; (13:8).
from the tribe of Benjamin, Palti son of Raphu; (13:9).
from the tribe of Zebulun, Gaddiel son of Sodi; (13:10).
from the tribe of Manasseh (a tribe of Joseph), Gaddi son of Susi; (13:11).
from the tribe of Dan, Ammiel son of Gemalli; (13:12).
from the tribe of Asher, Sethur son of Michael; (13:13).
from the tribe of Naphtali, Nahbi son of Vophsi; (13:14).
and from the tribe of Gad, Geuel son of Machi. (13:15).
These were the names of the men Moses sent to spy out the land; and Moses gave to Hoshea son of Nun the name Joshua. (13:16).
When Moses sent them to spy out the land of Canaan, he told them, “Go up through the Negev and into the hill country. (13:17).
See what the land is like and whether its people are strong or weak, few or many. (13:18).
Is the land where they live good or bad? Are the cities where they dwell open camps or fortifications? (13:19).
Is the soil fertile or unproductive? Are there trees in it or not? Be courageous and bring back some of the fruit of the land.” (It was the season for the first ripe grapes.) (13:20).
So they went up and spied out the land from the Wilderness of Zin as far as Rehob, toward Lebo-hamath. (13:21).
They went up through the Negev and came to Hebron, where Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai, the descendants of Anak, dwelled. It had been built seven years before Zoan in Egypt. (13:22).
When they came to the Valley of Eshcol, they cut down a branch with a single cluster of grapes, which they carried on a pole between two men. They also took some pomegranates and figs. (13:23).
Because of the cluster of grapes the Israelites cut there, that place was called the Valley of Eshcol. (13:24).
After forty days the men returned from spying out the land, (13:25).

and they went back to Moses, Aaron, and the whole congregation of Israel in the Wilderness of Paran at Kadesh. They brought back a report for the whole congregation and showed them the fruit of the land. (13:26).
And they gave this account to Moses: “We went into the land to which you sent us, and indeed, it is flowing with milk and honey. Here is some of its fruit! (13:27).
Nevertheless, the people living in the land are strong, and the cities are large and fortified. We even saw the descendants of Anak there. (13:28).
The Amalekites live in the land of the Negev; the Hittites, Jebusites, and Amorites live in the hill country; and the Canaanites live by the sea and along the Jordan.” (13:29).
Then Caleb quieted the people before Moses and said, “We must go up and take possession of the land, for we can certainly conquer it!” (13:30).
But the men who had gone up with him replied, “We cannot go up against the people, for they are stronger than we are!” (13:31).
So they gave the Israelites a bad report about the land that they had spied out: “The land we explored devours its inhabitants, and all the people we saw there are great in stature. (13:32).
We even saw the Nephilim there— the descendants of Anak that come from the Nephilim! We seemed like grasshoppers in our own sight, and we must have seemed the same to them!” (13:33).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 1:19-25: Moses retells the sending of the twelve men and the report that the land is good.
Joshua 14:6-12: Caleb at eighty-five recalls this journey and asks for the hill country he walked on.
Joshua 11:21-22: Joshua cuts off the Anakim from the hill country; none are left except in Gaza, Gath and Ashdod.
Genesis 23:2,19: Sarah is buried at Hebron, then called Kiriath-arba, in the cave of Machpelah.
1 Samuel 17:4: Goliath comes out from Gath, a champion whose height is six cubits and a span.

translationNotes.note: The Negev is the dry southern district of the land, not a sand desert but scrub and loess hills that get about 200 millimetres of rain a year in the north and almost none in the south. The word also came to mean south generally, which is why older versions sometimes read the south. The route in verse 17 runs from that dry country up into the hills, and the climb is real.

Hebron sits about 930 metres above sea level, the highest town in the land, in country good for vines and olives, which is why the spies cut grapes near it. Zoan is Tanis in the eastern Nile delta. Verse 22 dates Hebron seven years earlier than Zoan, and it is the only place in Scripture that dates a Canaanite town against an Egyptian one.

The name means cluster, and verse 24 says it was called that because of the cluster the men cut there. Carrying one bunch of grapes on a pole between two men is not exaggeration for weight alone: fruit brought back as legal evidence had to arrive undamaged, and slinging it kept it off the ground. The Hebron hills still produce grapes, figs and pomegranates, the three fruits verse 23 names.

A people of unusual height living around Hebron, whose three clan heads are named in verse 22 as Ahiman, Sheshai and Talmai. Deuteronomy 2:10-11 and 9:2 describe them the same way, and Joshua 11:22 records that the only Anakim left after the conquest were in the Philistine cities of Gaza, Gath and Ashdod, which is where Goliath of Gath comes from (1 Samuel 17:4).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: זָבַת חָלָב וּדְבָשׁ (zavat chalav u-devash)
translationNotes.note: Not a picture of luxury. Milk means herds that can be grazed year round, and honey in Hebrew usually means date or grape syrup as well as bee honey, meaning fruit trees that bear. The phrase describes land that supports both pasture and orchard without irrigation, which was the practical definition of good country. Even the men bringing the bad report concede it in verse 27.

stories.keyTakeaway: Moses sends twelve tribal leaders to scout Canaan for forty days; they return with fruit samples and confirm the land's fertility, but ten of them report that its inhabitants are too powerful to defeat, while Caleb insists Israel can take possession.

stories.title: 😠 Numbers 14
summaryBullets: Then the whole congregation lifted up their voices and cried out, and that night the people wept. (14:1).
All the Israelites grumbled against Moses and Aaron, and the whole congregation said to them, “If only we had died in the land of Egypt, or if only we had died in this wilderness! (14:2).
Why is the LORD bringing us into this land to fall by the sword? Our wives and children will become plunder. Would it not be better for us to go back to Egypt?” (14:3).
So they said to one another, “Let us appoint a leader and return to Egypt.” (14:4).
Then Moses and Aaron fell facedown before the whole assembly of the congregation of Israel. (14:5).
Joshua son of Nun and Caleb son of Jephunneh, who were among those who had spied out the land, tore their clothes (14:6).
and said to the whole congregation of Israel, “The land we passed through and explored is an exceedingly good land. (14:7).
If the LORD delights in us, He will bring us into this land, a land flowing with milk and honey, and He will give it to us. (14:8).

Only do not rebel against the LORD, and do not be afraid of the people of the land, for they will be like bread for us. Their protection has been removed, and the LORD is with us. Do not be afraid of them!” (14:9).
But the whole congregation threatened to stone Joshua and Caleb. Then the glory of the LORD appeared to all the Israelites at the Tent of Meeting. (14:10).
And the LORD said to Moses, “How long will this people treat Me with contempt? How long will they refuse to believe in Me, despite all the signs I have performed among them? (14:11).
I will strike them with a plague and destroy them — and I will make you into a nation greater and mightier than they are.” (14:12).
But Moses said to the LORD, “The Egyptians will hear of it, for by Your strength You brought this people from among them. (14:13).

And they will tell it to the inhabitants of this land. They have already heard that You, O LORD, are in the midst of this people, that You, O LORD, have been seen face to face, that Your cloud stands over them, and that You go before them in a pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night. (14:14).
If You kill this people as one man, the nations who have heard of Your fame will say, (14:15).
‘Because the LORD was unable to bring this people into the land He swore to give them, He has slaughtered them in the wilderness.’ (14:16).
So now I pray, may the power of my Lord be magnified, just as You have declared: (14:17).

‘The LORD is slow to anger and abounding in loving devotion, forgiving iniquity and transgression. Yet He will by no means leave the guilty unpunished; He will visit the iniquity of the fathers upon their children to the third and fourth generation.’ (14:18).
Pardon, I pray, the iniquity of this people, in keeping with the greatness of Your loving devotion, just as You have forgiven them ever since they left Egypt.” (14:19).
“I have pardoned them as you requested,” the LORD replied. (14:20).
“Yet as surely as I live and as surely as the whole earth is filled with the glory of the LORD, (14:21).
not one of the men who have seen My glory and the signs I performed in Egypt and in the wilderness — yet have tested Me and disobeyed Me these ten times — (14:22).
not one will ever see the land that I swore to give their fathers. None of those who have treated Me with contempt will see it. (14:23).
But because My servant Caleb has a different spirit and has followed Me wholeheartedly, I will bring him into the land he has entered, and his descendants will inherit it. (14:24).
Now since the Amalekites and Canaanites are living in the valleys, turn back tomorrow and head for the wilderness along the route to the Red Sea.” (14:25).
Then the LORD said to Moses and Aaron, (14:26).
“How long will this wicked congregation grumble against Me? I have heard the complaints that the Israelites are making against Me. (14:27).
