So tell them: As surely as I live, declares the LORD, I will do to you exactly as I heard you say. (14:28).
Your bodies will fall in this wilderness— all who were numbered in the census, everyone twenty years of age or older— because you have grumbled against Me. (14:29).
Surely none of you will enter the land in which I swore to settle you, except Caleb son of Jephunneh and Joshua son of Nun. (14:30).
But I will bring your children, whom you said would become plunder, into the land you have rejected — and they will enjoy it. (14:31).
As for you, however, your bodies will fall in this wilderness. (14:32).
Your children will be shepherds in the wilderness for forty years, and they will suffer for your unfaithfulness until the last of your bodies lies in the wilderness. (14:33).
In keeping with the forty days you spied out the land, you shall bear your guilt forty years — a year for each day — and you will experience My alienation. (14:34).

I, the LORD, have spoken, and I will surely do these things to this entire wicked congregation, which has conspired against Me. They will meet their end in the wilderness, and there they will die.” (14:35).
So the men Moses had sent to spy out the land, who had returned and made the whole congregation grumble against him by bringing out a bad report about the land— (14:36).
those men who had brought out the bad report about the land— were struck down by a plague before the LORD. (14:37).
Of those men who had gone to spy out the land, only Joshua son of Nun and Caleb son of Jephunneh remained alive. (14:38).
And when Moses relayed these words to all the Israelites, the people mourned bitterly. (14:39).
Early the next morning they got up and went up toward the ridge of the hill country. “We have indeed sinned,” they said, “but we will go to the place the LORD has promised.” (14:40).
But Moses said, “Why are you transgressing the commandment of the LORD? This will not succeed! (14:41).
Do not go up, lest you be struck down by your enemies, because the LORD is not among you. (14:42).
For there the Amalekites and Canaanites will face you, and you will fall by the sword. Because you have turned away from the LORD, He will not be with you.” (14:43).
But they dared to go up to the ridge of the hill country, though neither Moses nor the ark of the covenant of the LORD moved from the camp. (14:44).
Then the Amalekites and Canaanites who lived in that part of the hill country came down, attacked them, and routed them all the way to Hormah. (14:45).
crossRefs: Exodus 34:6-7: The LORD is slow to anger and abounding in loving devotion, the words Moses quotes back to Him.
Deuteronomy 1:34-40: God swears that not one of that evil generation will see the good land.
Psalm 95:8-11: Do not harden your hearts as at Meribah; forty years I was grieved with that generation.
Hebrews 3:16-19: They were unable to enter because of unbelief, arguing from Psalm 95.
1 Corinthians 10:1-11: These things happened as examples and were written down as warnings for us.

translationNotes.note: Ripping the outer garment was the public signal of grief or horror, done on the spot when the news landed. Jacob does it for Joseph (Genesis 37:34), David for Saul (2 Samuel 1:11), the high priest at Jesus' trial (Matthew 26:65). Joshua and Caleb do it here as the crowd talks about going back to Egypt, which marks what they are hearing as a disaster rather than a disagreement.

The sentence in verse 34 is measured out to match the offence: forty days of scouting becomes forty years of waiting. Deuteronomy 2:14 gives the accounting from the other end, thirty-eight years from Kadesh-barnea to the crossing of the Zered, once the two years already spent are set against the forty.

Peger means a dead body, usually one lying unburied. The phrase in verses 29 and 32 is blunt: your corpses will drop in this wilderness. Hebrews 3:17 quotes it directly, whose bodies fell in the wilderness. It applies to everyone counted in the census of chapter 1, that is, every man twenty and over except Caleb and Joshua.

The name is built on the root cherem, the ban or devotion to destruction, so the place where Israel is beaten and driven back carries the word for total destruction in its name. Numbers 21:3 records the same name given to a place after Israel devoted the Canaanites there, which is the reverse outcome at the reverse moment.

A nomadic raiding people of the Negev and northern Sinai, descended from Esau through Eliphaz (Genesis 36:12). They were the first nation to attack Israel after the exodus, striking the stragglers at the rear (Exodus 17:8-16; Deuteronomy 25:17-18), which is why war with Amalek is declared from generation to generation. Balaam calls them first among the nations at 24:20.

stories.keyTakeaway: The Israelites rebel against entering Canaan and plot to return to Egypt; Joshua and Caleb urge trust in God, but the assembly threatens to stone them. God decrees that all adults who doubted him will die in the wilderness over forty years, sparing only Joshua and Caleb, and the ten scouts who incited the rebellion are struck down by plague.

headings.text: The Plague on the Ten Spies

stories.title: 😠 Numbers 15
summaryBullets: Then the LORD said to Moses, (15:1).
“Speak to the Israelites and tell them: After you enter the land that I am giving you as a home (15:2).

and you present a food offering to the LORD from the herd or flock to produce a pleasing aroma to the LORD — either a burnt offering or a sacrifice, for a special vow or freewill offering or appointed feast— (15:3).
then the one presenting his offering to the LORD shall also present a grain offering of a tenth of an ephah of fine flour mixed with a quarter hin of olive oil. (15:4).
With the burnt offering or sacrifice of each lamb, you are to prepare a quarter hin of wine as a drink offering. (15:5).
With a ram you are to prepare a grain offering of two-tenths of an ephah of fine flour mixed with a third of a hin of olive oil, (15:6).
and a third of a hin of wine as a drink offering, a pleasing aroma to the LORD. (15:7).
When you prepare a young bull as a burnt offering or sacrifice to fulfill a vow or as a peace offering to the LORD, (15:8).
present with the bull a grain offering of three-tenths of an ephah of fine flour mixed with half a hin of olive oil. (15:9).
Also present half a hin of wine as a drink offering. It is a food offering, a pleasing aroma to the LORD. (15:10).
This is to be done for each bull, ram, lamb, or goat. (15:11).
This is how you must prepare each one, no matter how many. (15:12).
Everyone who is native-born shall prepare these things in this way when he presents a food offering as a pleasing aroma to the LORD. (15:13).
And for the generations to come, if a foreigner residing with you or someone else among you wants to prepare a food offering as a pleasing aroma to the LORD, he is to do exactly as you do. (15:14).

The assembly is to have the same statute both for you and for the foreign resident; it is a permanent statute for the generations to come. You and the foreigner shall be the same before the LORD. (15:15).
The same law and the same ordinance will apply both to you and to the foreigner residing with you.” (15:16).
Then the LORD said to Moses, (15:17).
“Speak to the Israelites and tell them: When you enter the land to which I am bringing you (15:18).
and you eat the food of the land, you shall lift up an offering to the LORD. (15:19).
From the first of your dough, you are to lift up a cake as a contribution; offer it just like an offering from the threshing floor. (15:20).
Throughout your generations, you are to give the LORD an offering from the first of your dough. (15:21).
Now if you stray unintentionally and do not obey all these commandments that the LORD has spoken to Moses— (15:22).
all that the LORD has commanded you through Moses from the day the LORD gave them and continuing through the generations to come— (15:23).

and if it was done unintentionally without the knowledge of the congregation, then the whole congregation is to prepare one young bull as a burnt offering, a pleasing aroma to the LORD, with its grain offering and drink offering according to the regulation, and one male goat as a sin offering. (15:24).

The priest is to make atonement for the whole congregation of Israel, so that they may be forgiven; for the sin was unintentional and they have brought to the LORD a food offering and a sin offering, presented before the LORD for their unintentional sin. (15:25).
Then the whole congregation of Israel and the foreigners residing among them will be forgiven, since it happened to all the people unintentionally. (15:26).
Also, if one person sins unintentionally, he is to present a year-old female goat as a sin offering. (15:27).
And the priest shall make atonement before the LORD on behalf of the person who erred by sinning unintentionally; and when atonement has been made for him, he will be forgiven. (15:28).
You shall have the same law for the one who acts in error, whether he is a native-born Israelite or a foreigner residing among you. (15:29).
But the person who sins defiantly, whether a native or foreigner, blasphemes the LORD. That person shall be cut off from among his people. (15:30).
He shall certainly be cut off, because he has despised the word of the LORD and broken His commandment; his guilt remains on him.” (15:31).
While the Israelites were in the wilderness, a man was found gathering wood on the Sabbath day. (15:32).
Those who found the man gathering wood brought him to Moses, Aaron, and the whole congregation, (15:33).
and because it had not been declared what should be done to him, they placed him in custody. (15:34).
And the LORD said to Moses, “The man must surely be put to death. The whole congregation is to stone him outside the camp.” (15:35).
So the whole congregation took the man outside the camp and stoned him to death, as the LORD had commanded Moses. (15:36).
And the LORD said to Moses, (15:37).
“Speak to the Israelites and tell them that throughout the generations to come they are to make for themselves tassels for the corners of their garments, with a blue cord on each tassel. (15:38).

These will serve as tassels for you to look at, so that you may remember all the commandments of the LORD, that you may obey them and not prostitute yourselves by following your own heart and your own eyes. (15:39).
Then you will remember and obey all My commandments, and you will be holy to your God. (15:40).
I am the LORD your God who brought you out of the land of Egypt to be your God. I am the LORD your God.” (15:41).
crossRefs: Leviticus 4:1-2,27-31: The sin offering prescribed for a person who sins unintentionally.
Deuteronomy 22:12: Make tassels on the four corners of the cloak you wear.
Matthew 9:20-21: A woman touches the tassel of Jesus' cloak, believing that will be enough to heal her.
Matthew 23:5: They widen their phylacteries and lengthen the tassels of their garments to be seen.
Exodus 31:14-15: Whoever profanes the Sabbath must surely be put to death.

translationNotes.note: The ephah is the standard dry measure, about 22 litres or roughly two thirds of a bushel; a tenth of an ephah, about 2.2 litres, is one person's daily grain and is the omer of Exodus 16:36. The hin is the standard liquid measure, about 3.7 litres or a gallon. So the offering with one lamb is roughly two litres of flour, a litre of oil and a litre of wine, and the amounts scale up with the size of the animal.

Knotted cords tied at the four corners of the outer garment, with one cord of blue in each. Verse 39 gives the purpose in plain terms: they are there to be looked at, so that a man seeing them remembers the commandments. Deuteronomy 22:12 repeats the command. This is the fringe a woman reaches for in Matthew 9:20, and the one Jesus says the Pharisees make too long in Matthew 23:5.

A blue-violet dye taken from a sea snail, Hexaplex trunculus, gathered on the Phoenician coast. It took thousands of snails to produce a small quantity, which made it one of the most expensive substances in the ancient world and the colour of royalty and of the tabernacle hangings. Mounds of crushed dye shells and the remains of dye vats have been excavated at Tel Shikmona and along the Lebanese coast. A single blue thread in a working man's hem was a real expense.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בְּיָד רָמָה (be-yad ramah), with a high hand
translationNotes.note: The Hebrew is with a raised hand, the gesture of open defiance. The chapter divides offences in two: what is done by mistake has a sacrifice attached to it, and what is done deliberately, in the face of the command, has none. The text says such a person blasphemes and is cut off (15:30-31), and the wood-gatherer of verses 32 to 36 follows immediately as the worked example.

A portion lifted out of the first batch of dough from each harvest's grain and given as a contribution (15:20-21). The word challah is the loaf itself, and it is the origin of the name still used for the braided sabbath bread. Nehemiah 10:37 lists it among the dues the returning exiles bound themselves to bring.

stories.keyTakeaway: God prescribes the grain and drink offerings to accompany animal sacrifices, applies the same rules to foreigners as to native Israelites, and establishes procedures for atonement when the community unintentionally breaks his commands. A man caught gathering wood on the Sabbath is stoned to death, and God commands the Israelites to wear tassels on their garments as reminders to obey his commands.

stories.title: 😠 Numbers 16
summaryBullets: Now Korah son of Izhar, the son of Kohath son of Levi, along with some Reubenites — Dathan and Abiram, sons of Eliab, and On son of Peleth — conducted (16:1).
a rebellion against Moses, along with 250 men of Israel renowned as leaders of the congregation and representatives in the assembly. (16:2).

They came together against Moses and Aaron and told them, “You have taken too much upon yourselves! For everyone in the entire congregation is holy, and the LORD is in their midst. Why then do you exalt yourselves above the assembly of the LORD?” (16:3).
When Moses heard this, he fell facedown. (16:4).

Then he said to Korah and all his followers, “Tomorrow morning the LORD will reveal who belongs to Him and who is holy, and He will bring that person near to Himself. The one He chooses He will bring near to Himself. (16:5).
You, Korah, and all your followers are to do as follows: Take censers, (16:6).

and tomorrow you are to place fire and incense in them in the presence of the LORD. Then the man the LORD chooses will be the one who is holy. It is you sons of Levi who have taken too much upon yourselves!” (16:7).
Moses also said to Korah, “Now listen, you sons of Levi! (16:8).

Is it not enough for you that the God of Israel has separated you from the congregation of Israel and brought you near to Himself to perform the work at the LORD’s tabernacle, and to stand before the congregation to minister to them? (16:9).
He has brought you near, you and all your fellow Levites, but you are seeking the priesthood as well. (16:10).
Therefore, it is you and all your followers who have conspired against the LORD! As for Aaron, who is he that you should grumble against him?” (16:11).
Then Moses summoned Dathan and Abiram, the sons of Eliab, but they said, “We will not come! (16:12).
Is it not enough that you have brought us up out of a land flowing with milk and honey to kill us in the wilderness? Must you also appoint yourself as ruler over us? (16:13).
Moreover, you have not brought us into a land flowing with milk and honey or given us an inheritance of fields and vineyards. Will you gouge out the eyes of these men? No, we will not come!” (16:14).
Then Moses became very angry and said to the LORD, “Do not regard their offering. I have not taken one donkey from them or mistreated a single one of them.” (16:15).
And Moses said to Korah, “You and all your followers are to appear before the LORD tomorrow— you and they and Aaron. (16:16).
Each man is to take his censer, place incense in it, and present it before the LORD— 250 censers. You and Aaron are to present your censers as well.” (16:17).
So each man took his censer, put fire and incense in it, and stood with Moses and Aaron at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting. (16:18).
When Korah had gathered his whole assembly against them at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting, the glory of the LORD appeared to the whole congregation. (16:19).
And the LORD said to Moses and Aaron, (16:20).
“Separate yourselves from this congregation so that I may consume them in an instant.” (16:21).
But Moses and Aaron fell facedown and said, “O God, the God of the spirits of all flesh, when one man sins, will You be angry with the whole congregation?” (16:22).
Then the LORD said to Moses, (16:23).
“Tell the congregation to move away from the dwellings of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram.” (16:24).
So Moses got up and went to Dathan and Abiram, and the elders of Israel followed him. (16:25).
And he warned the congregation, “Move away now from the tents of these wicked men. Do not touch anything that belongs to them, or you will be swept away because of all their sins.” (16:26).

So they moved away from the dwellings of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram. Meanwhile, Dathan and Abiram had come out and stood at the entrances to their tents with their wives and children and infants. (16:27).
Then Moses said, “This is how you will know that the LORD has sent me to do all these things, for it was not my own doing: (16:28).
If these men die a natural death, or if they suffer the fate of all men, then the LORD has not sent me. (16:29).

But if the LORD brings about something unprecedented, and the earth opens its mouth and swallows them and all that belongs to them so that they go down alive into Sheol, then you will know that these men have treated the LORD with contempt.” (16:30).
As soon as Moses had finished saying all this, the ground beneath them split open, (16:31).
and the earth opened its mouth and swallowed them and their households — all Korah’s men and all their possessions. (16:32).
They went down alive into Sheol with all they owned. The earth closed over them, and they vanished from the assembly. (16:33).
At their cries, all the people of Israel who were around them fled, saying, “The earth may swallow us too!” (16:34).
And fire came forth from the LORD and consumed the 250 men who were offering the incense. (16:35).
Then the LORD said to Moses, (16:36).
“Tell Eleazar son of Aaron the priest to remove the censers from the flames and to scatter the coals far away, because the censers are holy. (16:37).

As for the censers of those who sinned at the cost of their own lives, hammer them into sheets to overlay the altar, for these were presented before the LORD, and so have become holy. They will serve as a sign to the Israelites.” (16:38).
So Eleazar the priest took the bronze censers brought by those who had been burned up, and he had them hammered out to overlay the altar, (16:39).

just as the LORD commanded him through Moses. This was to be a reminder to the Israelites that no outsider who is not a descendant of Aaron should approach to offer incense before the LORD, lest he become like Korah and his followers. (16:40).
The next day the whole congregation of Israel grumbled against Moses and Aaron, saying, “You have killed the LORD’s people!” (16:41).
But when the congregation gathered against them, Moses and Aaron turned toward the Tent of Meeting, and suddenly the cloud covered it and the glory of the LORD appeared. (16:42).
Then Moses and Aaron went to the front of the Tent of Meeting, (16:43).
and the LORD said to Moses, (16:44).
“Get away from this congregation so that I may consume them in an instant.” And Moses and Aaron fell facedown. (16:45).

Moses said to Aaron, “Take your censer, place fire from the altar in it, and add incense. Go quickly to the congregation and make atonement for them, because wrath has come out from the LORD; the plague has begun.” (16:46).

So Aaron took the censer as Moses had ordered and ran into the midst of the assembly. And seeing that the plague had begun among the people, he offered the incense and made atonement for the people. (16:47).
He stood between the living and the dead, and the plague was halted. (16:48).
But those who died from the plague numbered 14,700, in addition to those who had died on account of Korah. (16:49).
Then Aaron returned to Moses at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting, since the plague had been halted. (16:50).
crossRefs: Exodus 6:16-21: The line of Levi through Kohath and Izhar, the family Korah belongs to.
Numbers 26:9-11: Dathan and Abiram swallowed up as a warning sign, but the line of Korah did not die out.
Psalm 106:16-18: The earth opened and swallowed Dathan and covered the company of Abiram.
Jude 1:11: Woe to them, for they have perished in Korah's rebellion.
2 Chronicles 26:16-21: King Uzziah burns incense in the temple, is opposed by the priests, and is struck with disease.

translationNotes.note: A shallow bronze fire pan with a handle, used to carry live coals from the altar and burn incense on them. Only priests handled them (Leviticus 16:12). The 250 men who take up censers here are staging a claim to the priesthood, not a protest, which is why Moses answers with a test involving censers. Aaron uses one in verses 46 to 48 to stop the plague.

Korah is not an outsider. He is a Kohathite, from the clan that carried the ark and the holy vessels (4:4-15), so his family already had the highest-status task in the camp short of the priesthood. Moses says so directly in verses 9 and 10. The Reubenites Dathan and Abiram have a separate grievance, stated in verses 13 and 14, about leadership and land, and the chapter keeps the two complaints apart.

Sheol is the Hebrew name for the realm of the dead, thought of as beneath the ground. The phrase means they went there without dying first in any ordinary way, which is the sign Moses asks for in verse 30 to settle whether he was sent. Psalm 55:15 borrows the phrase, and Numbers 26:10 calls the whole event a sign.

translationNotes.term: Hammered into sheets for the altar
translationNotes.note: The 250 bronze censers were beaten flat and fixed as plating on the altar, because they had been brought before the LORD and could not go back to ordinary use (16:37-40). Verse 40 states the purpose: a permanent reminder that no one outside Aaron's line approaches to burn incense. The altar itself carried the evidence of what had happened at it.

The dead from the plague the following day, in addition to those who died with Korah (16:49). Aaron running into the middle of the assembly with a censer, standing between the living and the dead, is the act that halts it. The number is given without comment, which is how this book records its tolls: 14,700 here, 24,000 at Peor (25:9), and no words spent on either.

stories.keyTakeaway: Korah, Dathan, Abiram, and 250 community leaders rebel against Moses and Aaron's authority; the earth swallows Korah's group alive and fire consumes the 250 men, yet the next day the assembly grumbles again and a plague kills 14,700 more before Aaron makes atonement.

headings.text: The Censers Reserved for Holy Use

stories.title: 😠 Numbers 17
summaryBullets: And the LORD said to Moses, (17:1).
“Speak to the Israelites and take from them twelve staffs, one from the leader of each tribe. Write each man’s name on his staff, (17:2).
and write Aaron’s name on the staff of Levi, because there must be one staff for the head of each tribe. (17:3).
Place the staffs in the Tent of Meeting in front of the Testimony, where I meet with you. (17:4).
The staff belonging to the man I choose will sprout, and I will rid Myself of the constant grumbling of the Israelites against you.” (17:5).
So Moses spoke to the Israelites, and each of their leaders gave him a staff — one for each of the leaders of their tribes, twelve staffs in all. And Aaron’s staff was among them. (17:6).
Then Moses placed the staffs before the LORD in the Tent of the Testimony. (17:7).
The next day Moses entered the Tent of the Testimony and saw that Aaron’s staff, representing the house of Levi, had sprouted, put forth buds, blossomed, and produced almonds. (17:8).
Then Moses brought out all the staffs from the LORD’s presence to all the Israelites. They saw them, and each man took his own staff. (17:9).
The LORD said to Moses, “Put Aaron’s staff back in front of the Testimony, to be kept as a sign for the rebellious, so that you may put an end to their grumbling against Me, lest they die.” (17:10).
So Moses did as the LORD had commanded him. (17:11).
Then the Israelites declared to Moses, “Look, we are perishing! We are lost; we are all lost! (17:12).
Anyone who comes near the tabernacle of the LORD will die. Are we all going to perish?” (17:13).
crossRefs: Hebrews 9:4: The ark contained the gold jar of manna, Aaron's staff that had budded, and the tablets of the covenant.
Exodus 16:32-34: A jar of manna kept before the Testimony as a record for the generations to come.
Jeremiah 1:11-12: The branch of an almond tree, and the wordplay on God watching over His word to perform it.
Ezekiel 7:10: The rod has budded, arrogance has blossomed.
Numbers 16:1-11: The challenge to Aaron's priesthood that this sign is answering.

translationNotes.note: The same Hebrew word means a staff and a tribe, and the whole chapter turns on that. Twelve matteh are collected, one per matteh, with each leader's name written on it. English has to choose one word and the pun disappears completely. A leader's staff was his badge of office, cut and carried personally, which is what makes each one identifiable in verse 9.

The almond is the first tree in the land to flower, blossoming in late January or February while everything else is bare, and its name puns with shoqed, watching or being awake. Jeremiah 1:11-12 uses that pun outright. A staff that goes from bare wood to bud, blossom and ripe fruit overnight compresses a whole season of the earliest-waking tree into one night.

The staff is put back in front of the Testimony and stored permanently, in the same place as the jar of manna (Exodus 16:33-34). Hebrews 9:4 lists all three items together: the jar of manna, Aaron's budded staff and the tablets. These were the physical archive of the disputes God had already settled, kept where the disputes had been settled.

The people's reaction in verses 12 and 13 is not repentance but panic about proximity: anyone who comes near the tabernacle dies, so are we all going to die? Chapter 18 opens as the direct answer to that question, assigning the Levites as the buffer who bear the risk on everyone else's behalf. The chapter division cuts a single exchange in half.

stories.keyTakeaway: God instructs Moses to collect twelve staffs from the tribal leaders, place them in the tent of meeting, and declares that the staff of his chosen leader will sprout; the next day Aaron's staff has budded, blossomed, and produced almonds. Moses returns Aaron's staff to the ark as a sign to silence the Israelites' complaints, though they respond with fear that they will die for approaching the tabernacle.

stories.title: 😠 Numbers 18
summaryBullets: So the LORD said to Aaron, “You and your sons and your father’s house must bear the iniquity involving the sanctuary. And you and your sons alone must bear the iniquity involving your priesthood. (18:1).
But bring with you also your brothers from the tribe of Levi, the tribe of your father, that they may join you and assist you and your sons before the Tent of the Testimony. (18:2).
And they shall attend to your duties and to all the duties of the Tent; but they must not come near to the furnishings of the sanctuary or the altar, or both they and you will die. (18:3).
They are to join you and attend to the duties of the Tent of Meeting, doing all the work at the Tent; but no outsider may come near you. (18:4).
And you shall attend to the duties of the sanctuary and of the altar, so that wrath may not fall on the Israelites again. (18:5).
Behold, I Myself have selected your fellow Levites from the Israelites as a gift to you, dedicated to the LORD to perform the service for the Tent of Meeting. (18:6).

But only you and your sons shall attend to your priesthood for everything concerning the altar and what is inside the veil, and you are to perform that service. I am giving you the work of the priesthood as a gift, but any outsider who comes near the sanctuary must be put to death.” (18:7).

Then the LORD said to Aaron, “Behold, I have put you in charge of My offerings. As for all the sacred offerings of the Israelites, I have given them to you and your sons as a portion and a permanent statute. (18:8).

A portion of the most holy offerings reserved from the fire will be yours. From all the offerings they render to Me as most holy offerings, whether grain offerings or sin offerings or guilt offerings, that part belongs to you and your sons. (18:9).
You are to eat it as a most holy offering, and every male may eat it. You shall regard it as holy. (18:10).

And this is yours as well: the offering of their gifts, along with all the wave offerings of the Israelites. I have given this to you and your sons and daughters as a permanent statute. Every ceremonially clean person in your household may eat it. (18:11).
I give you all the freshest olive oil and all the finest new wine and grain that the Israelites give to the LORD as their firstfruits. (18:12).
The firstfruits of everything in their land that they bring to the LORD will belong to you. Every ceremonially clean person in your household may eat them. (18:13).
Every devoted thing in Israel belongs to you. (18:14).
The firstborn of every womb, whether man or beast, that is offered to the LORD belongs to you. But you must surely redeem every firstborn son and every firstborn male of unclean animals. (18:15).
You are to pay the redemption price for a month-old male according to your valuation: five shekels of silver, according to the sanctuary shekel, which is twenty gerahs. (18:16).

But you must not redeem the firstborn of an ox, a sheep, or a goat; they are holy. You are to splatter their blood on the altar and burn their fat as a food offering, a pleasing aroma to the LORD. (18:17).
And their meat belongs to you, just as the breast and right thigh of the wave offering belong to you. (18:18).

All the holy offerings that the Israelites present to the LORD I give to you and to your sons and daughters as a permanent statute. It is a permanent covenant of salt before the LORD for you and your offspring.” (18:19).
Then the LORD said to Aaron, “You will have no inheritance in their land, nor will you have any portion among them. I am your portion and your inheritance among the Israelites. (18:20).
Behold, I have given to the Levites all the tithes in Israel as an inheritance in return for the work they do, the service of the Tent of Meeting. (18:21).
No longer may the Israelites come near to the Tent of Meeting, or they will incur guilt and die. (18:22).

The Levites are to perform the work of the Tent of Meeting, and they must bear their iniquity. This is a permanent statute for the generations to come. The Levites will not receive an inheritance among the Israelites. (18:23).

For I have given to the Levites as their inheritance the tithe that the Israelites present to the LORD as a contribution. That is why I told them that they would not receive an inheritance among the Israelites.” (18:24).
And the LORD instructed Moses, (18:25).

“Speak to the Levites and tell them: ‘When you receive from the Israelites the tithe that I have given you as your inheritance, you must present part of it as an offering to the LORD— a tithe of the tithe. (18:26).
Your offering will be reckoned to you as grain from the threshing floor or juice from the winepress. (18:27).
So you are to present an offering to the LORD from all the tithes you receive from the Israelites, and from these you are to give the LORD’s offering to Aaron the priest. (18:28).
You must present the offering due the LORD from all the best of every gift, the holiest part of it.’ (18:29).
Therefore say to the Levites, ‘When you have presented the best part, it will be reckoned to you as the produce of the threshing floor or winepress. (18:30).
And you and your households may eat the rest of it anywhere; it is the compensation for your work at the Tent of Meeting. (18:31).
Once you have presented the best part of it, you will not incur guilt because of it. But you must not defile the sacred offerings of the Israelites, or else you will die.’” (18:32).
crossRefs: Leviticus 27:30-33: A tenth of the produce of the land and of the herd and flock belongs to the LORD.
Deuteronomy 18:1-5: The priests and Levites have no allotment; they live on the offerings made to the LORD.
Nehemiah 10:37-39: The people bring their tithes to the Levites, and the Levites bring a tenth of the tithe to the priests.
Leviticus 2:13: Season every grain offering with salt; never leave the salt of the covenant out.
1 Corinthians 9:13-14: Those who serve at the altar share in the offerings of the altar.

translationNotes.note: Every other tribe received a block of territory. Levi received none, and verse 20 says the LORD is their portion instead. In an economy where land was the only capital and it stayed in the family across generations, this made the priests and Levites structurally dependent on the offerings of everyone else. They were given forty-eight towns to live in with pasture around them (35:1-8), but no tribal territory.

The Levites receive the tithe from Israel, and then hand a tenth of what they receive to the priests (18:26). It is a two-stage system and the second stage is not optional. Nehemiah 10:38 records a priest going with the Levites when they collected, precisely so the second tithe was taken. Malachi 3:8-10 is about the failure of that chain.

Salt preserves, so an agreement sealed with salt was one meant to last. Every grain offering had to be salted (Leviticus 2:13), and 2 Chronicles 13:5 says God gave the kingship to David by a covenant of salt. Salt was cut in blocks from the shore of the Dead Sea, which is where the ordinary supply came from. The phrase here means the priests' portion is permanent and not renegotiable.

Cherem is something irrevocably handed over, taken out of ordinary use forever. Applied to a city in war it means total destruction (Deuteronomy 7:2); applied to property here it means it goes to the priests and can never be bought back (Leviticus 27:28). The same word covers both because the core idea is not destruction but no return.

translationNotes.term: Five shekels for a firstborn son
translationNotes.note: A firstborn son is bought back at five sanctuary shekels, about 57 grams of silver, payable from one month old (18:16). Clean animals, an ox, a sheep or a goat, are not redeemed at all; they go to the altar. A donkey, which is unclean, is redeemed with a lamb or has its neck broken (Exodus 13:13). The system distinguishes what can be offered from what cannot.

stories.keyTakeaway: God assigns Aaron and his sons as priests with sole responsibility for the sanctuary and altar, grants them portions of Israel's holy offerings and firstfruits as perpetual payment, and designates the Levites as their assistants who will receive the people's tithes in exchange for their tent service.

stories.title: 😠 Numbers 19
summaryBullets: Then the LORD said to Moses and Aaron, (19:1).
“This is the statute of the law that the LORD has commanded: Instruct the Israelites to bring you an unblemished red heifer that has no defect and has never been placed under a yoke. (19:2).
Give it to Eleazar the priest, and he will have it brought outside the camp and slaughtered in his presence. (19:3).
Eleazar the priest is to take some of its blood on his finger and sprinkle it seven times toward the front of the Tent of Meeting. (19:4).
Then the heifer must be burned in his sight. Its hide, its flesh, and its blood are to be burned, along with its dung. (19:5).
The priest is to take cedar wood, hyssop, and scarlet wool and throw them onto the burning heifer. (19:6).
Then the priest must wash his clothes and bathe his body in water; after that he may enter the camp, but he will be ceremonially unclean until evening. (19:7).
The one who burned the heifer must also wash his clothes and bathe his body in water, and he too will be ceremonially unclean until evening. (19:8).

Then a man who is ceremonially clean is to gather up the ashes of the heifer and store them in a ceremonially clean place outside the camp. They must be kept by the congregation of Israel for preparing the water of purification; this is for purification from sin. (19:9).

The man who has gathered up the ashes of the heifer must also wash his clothes, and he will be ceremonially unclean until evening. This is a permanent statute for the Israelites and for the foreigner residing among them. (19:10).
Whoever touches any dead body will be unclean for seven days. (19:11).
He must purify himself with the water on the third day and on the seventh day; then he will be clean. But if he does not purify himself on the third and seventh days, he will not be clean. (19:12).

Anyone who touches a human corpse and fails to purify himself defiles the tabernacle of the LORD. That person must be cut off from Israel. He remains unclean, because the water of purification has not been sprinkled on him, and his uncleanness is still on him. (19:13).
This is the law when a person dies in a tent: Everyone who enters the tent and everyone already in the tent will be unclean for seven days, (19:14).
and any open container without a lid fastened on it is unclean. (19:15).
Anyone in the open field who touches someone who has been killed by the sword or has died of natural causes, or anyone who touches a human bone or a grave, will be unclean for seven days. (19:16).
For the purification of the unclean person, take some of the ashes of the burnt sin offering, put them in a jar, and pour fresh water over them. (19:17).

Then a man who is ceremonially clean is to take some hyssop, dip it in the water, and sprinkle the tent, all the furnishings, and the people who were there. He is also to sprinkle the one who touched a bone, a grave, or a person who has died or been slain. (19:18).

The man who is ceremonially clean is to sprinkle the unclean person on the third day and on the seventh day. After he purifies the unclean person on the seventh day, the one being cleansed must wash his clothes and bathe in water, and that evening he will be clean. (19:19).

But if a person who is unclean does not purify himself, he will be cut off from the assembly, because he has defiled the sanctuary of the LORD. The water of purification has not been sprinkled on him; he is unclean. (19:20).

This is a permanent statute for the people: The one who sprinkles the water of purification must wash his clothes, and whoever touches the water of purification will be unclean until evening. (19:21).
Anything the unclean person touches will become unclean, and anyone who touches it will be unclean until evening.” (19:22).
crossRefs: Leviticus 16:27-28: The bull and goat of the sin offering are carried outside the camp and burned.
Exodus 12:22: Take a bunch of hyssop, dip it in the blood, and strike the lintel and the two doorposts.
Psalm 51:7: Purify me with hyssop and I will be clean; wash me and I will be whiter than snow.
Hebrews 9:13-14: The ashes of a heifer sprinkled on those who are unclean sanctify for the cleansing of the flesh.
Numbers 31:19-24: The seven-day purification with this water applied to the army returning from Midian.

translationNotes.note: A young cow, red, without defect, that has never worn a yoke. The colour requirement appears nowhere else in the law, and the animal is not killed at the altar but outside the camp, and is burned whole: hide, flesh, blood and dung together (19:5). Its ashes were kept in a clean place outside the camp and mixed into water as needed. This is the one rite in the law whose whole purpose is cleansing after contact with a corpse.

Literally water of separation, made by mixing the stored ashes with fresh running water in a vessel (19:17). It was sprinkled with a hyssop bunch on the third day and again on the seventh. Skipping it did not merely leave a person unclean; verse 13 says the tabernacle itself was defiled and the person was cut off. In a camp of this size with people dying every week, this was routine and constant work.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֵץ אֶרֶז ('ets erez) - אֵזוֹב (ezov) - שְׁנִי תוֹלַעַת (sheni tola'at)
translationNotes.note: The same three materials appear in the cleansing of a person healed of a skin disease (Leviticus 14:4). Hyssop is a small aromatic herb of the oregano family that grows out of rock walls, with a bushy head that holds liquid, which is why it is the sprinkler in Exodus 12:22 and Psalm 51:7. The scarlet is wool dyed with the crimson grub. All three go into the fire with the heifer.

translationNotes.term: Anyone who touches a dead body
translationNotes.note: Death was the most contagious uncleanness in the system. It passed to anyone who touched a corpse, a bone or a grave, to everyone inside a tent where someone died, and to every open vessel in that tent that had no lid tied on (19:14-16). This is the reason a Nazirite may not go near a corpse even for a parent (6:7), the reason the priest and the Levite in Luke 10:31-32 pass by on the other side, and the reason there is a second Passover date in 9:10.

Everyone who handles the rite is defiled by it: the priest who sprinkles the blood, the man who burns the heifer, the man who gathers the ashes, and the man who later sprinkles the water (19:7-10,21). The thing that cleanses the unclean makes the clean unclean. The text states it as a standing rule and does not explain it.

stories.keyTakeaway: God instructs Moses and Aaron on a purification ritual using a red heifer; its ashes are mixed with water to cleanse those who touch corpses, with specific protocols for sprinkling on the third and seventh days.

stories.title: 😠 Numbers 20
summaryBullets: In the first month, the whole congregation of Israel entered the Wilderness of Zin and stayed in Kadesh. There Miriam died and was buried. (20:1).
Now there was no water for the congregation, so they gathered against Moses and Aaron. (20:2).
The people quarreled with Moses and said, “If only we had perished with our brothers before the LORD! (20:3).
Why have you brought the LORD’s assembly into this wilderness for us and our livestock to die here? (20:4).
Why have you led us up out of Egypt to bring us to this wretched place? It is not a place of grain, figs, vines, or pomegranates — and there is no water to drink!” (20:5).
Then Moses and Aaron went from the presence of the assembly to the entrance to the Tent of Meeting. They fell facedown, and the glory of the LORD appeared to them. (20:6).
And the LORD said to Moses, (20:7).

“Take the staff and assemble the congregation. You and your brother Aaron are to speak to the rock while they watch, and it will pour out its water. You will bring out water from the rock and provide drink for the congregation and their livestock.” (20:8).
So Moses took the staff from the LORD’s presence, just as he had been commanded. (20:9).
Then Moses and Aaron gathered the assembly in front of the rock, and Moses said to them, “Listen now, you rebels, must we bring you water out of this rock?” (20:10).
Then Moses raised his hand and struck the rock twice with his staff, so that a great amount of water gushed out, and the congregation and their livestock were able to drink. (20:11).

But the LORD said to Moses and Aaron, “Because you did not trust Me to show My holiness in the sight of the Israelites, you will not bring this assembly into the land that I have given them.” (20:12).
These were the waters of Meribah, where the Israelites quarreled with the LORD, and He showed His holiness among them. (20:13).
From Kadesh, Moses sent messengers to tell the king of Edom, “This is what your brother Israel says: You know all the hardship that has befallen us, (20:14).
how our fathers went down to Egypt, where we lived many years. The Egyptians mistreated us and our fathers, (20:15).
and when we cried out to the LORD, He heard our voice, sent an angel, and brought us out of Egypt. Now look, we are in Kadesh, a city on the edge of your territory. (20:16).

Please let us pass through your land. We will not go through any field or vineyard, or drink water from any well. We will stay on the King’s Highway; we will not turn to the right or to the left until we have passed through your territory.” (20:17).
But Edom answered, “You may not travel through our land, or we will come out and confront you with the sword.” (20:18).
“We will stay on the main road,” the Israelites replied, “and if we or our herds drink your water, we will pay for it. There will be no problem; only let us pass through on foot.” (20:19).
But Edom insisted, “You may not pass through.” And they came out to confront the Israelites with a large army and a strong hand. (20:20).
So Edom refused to allow Israel to pass through their territory, and Israel turned away from them. (20:21).
After they had set out from Kadesh, the whole congregation of Israel came to Mount Hor. (20:22).
And at Mount Hor, near the border of the land of Edom, the LORD said to Moses and Aaron, (20:23).
“Aaron will be gathered to his people; he will not enter the land that I have given the Israelites, because both of you rebelled against My command at the waters of Meribah. (20:24).
Take Aaron and his son Eleazar and bring them up Mount Hor. (20:25).
Remove Aaron’s priestly garments and put them on his son Eleazar. Aaron will be gathered to his people and will die there.” (20:26).
So Moses did as the LORD had commanded, and they climbed Mount Hor in the sight of the whole congregation. (20:27).
After Moses had removed Aaron’s garments and put them on his son Eleazar, Aaron died there on top of the mountain. Then Moses and Eleazar came down from the mountain. (20:28).
When the whole congregation saw that Aaron had died, the entire house of Israel mourned for him thirty days. (20:29).
crossRefs: Exodus 17:1-7: Moses strikes the rock at Horeb and water comes out, at the place called Massah and Meribah.
Psalm 106:32-33: They angered Him at the waters of Meribah, and it went badly for Moses because of them.
Deuteronomy 2:1-8: Israel turns aside from Edom and is told not to provoke the sons of Esau.
Genesis 25:24-26: Esau and Jacob born twins, the brotherhood Moses appeals to in his message to Edom.
Numbers 33:38-39: Aaron dies on Mount Hor in the fortieth year, at the age of 123.

translationNotes.note: Kadesh-barnea is the oasis where Israel spent most of the wilderness years, in the desert south of Canaan; it is generally identified with Ain el-Qudeirat in northeastern Sinai, the largest spring in that whole region. Deuteronomy 1:2 measures it at eleven days' walk from Horeb by the Mount Seir road. It sits roughly 120 kilometres southwest of Hebron, which is the distance the spies of chapter 13 covered.

The name means quarrelling, from the legal word riv, a lawsuit. Verse 13 says the place was named for the Israelites quarrelling with the LORD. There is an earlier Meribah near Horeb at the start of the wanderings (Exodus 17:7), where Moses was told to strike the rock; here, thirty-eight years later, he was told to speak to it and struck it twice instead.

Edom is the mountainous country south and east of the Dead Sea, settled by the descendants of Esau (Genesis 36:8-9). Its highlands rise above 1,500 metres and its passes are narrow and easy to hold, which is why an armed refusal at the border ends the argument. Israel was forbidden to take any of it (Deuteronomy 2:4-5), so the only option was the long detour south described at 21:4.

The main north-south road east of the Jordan, running from the Gulf of Aqaba up through Edom, Moab and Ammon to Damascus. It carried the caravan trade and it was the only route through that country that a large body could use, because the alternative is crossing a series of deep gorges. Israel asks for it again from Sihon at 21:22 and is refused again.

Thirty days is the mourning period for a national figure. Israel mourns Aaron thirty days here and Moses thirty days at Deuteronomy 34:8; the ordinary period for a family death was seven (Genesis 50:10). Aaron's priestly garments are transferred to Eleazar on the mountain before he dies (20:26), so the office passes without a gap, which is the practical point of the scene.

stories.keyTakeaway: Miriam dies at Kadesh; when the community complains about lack of water, Moses strikes a rock twice instead of speaking to it as commanded, and God says this act of distrust means neither Moses nor Aaron will enter the promised land. At Mount Hor, Aaron's priestly garments are transferred to his son Eleazar and Aaron dies there; the community mourns him for thirty days.

stories.title: 🐍 Numbers 21
summaryBullets: When the Canaanite king of Arad, who lived in the Negev, heard that Israel was coming along the road to Atharim, he attacked Israel and captured some prisoners. (21:1).
So Israel made a vow to the LORD: “If You will deliver this people into our hands, we will devote their cities to destruction.” (21:2).
And the LORD heard Israel’s plea and delivered up the Canaanites. Israel devoted them and their cities to destruction; so they named the place Hormah. (21:3).
Then they set out from Mount Hor along the route to the Red Sea, in order to bypass the land of Edom. But the people grew impatient on the journey (21:4).
and spoke against God and against Moses: “Why have you led us up out of Egypt to die in the wilderness? There is no bread or water, and we detest this wretched food!” (21:5).
So the LORD sent venomous snakes among the people, and many of the Israelites were bitten and died. (21:6).

Then the people came to Moses and said, “We have sinned by speaking against the LORD and against you. Intercede with the LORD so He will take the snakes away from us.” So Moses interceded for the people. (21:7).
Then the LORD said to Moses, “Make a fiery serpent and mount it on a pole. When anyone who is bitten looks at it, he will live.” (21:8).
So Moses made a bronze snake and mounted it on a pole. If anyone who was bitten looked at the bronze snake, he would live. (21:9).
Then the Israelites set out and camped at Oboth. (21:10).
They journeyed from Oboth and camped at Iye-abarim in the wilderness opposite Moab to the east. (21:11).
From there they set out and camped in the Valley of Zered. (21:12).

From there they moved on and camped on the other side of the Arnon, in the wilderness that extends into the Amorite territory. Now the Arnon is the border between the Moabites and the Amorites. (21:13).
Therefore it is stated in the Book of the Wars of the LORD: “Waheb in Suphah and the wadis of the Arnon, (21:14).
even the slopes of the wadis that extend to the site of Ar and lie along the border of Moab.” (21:15).
From there they went on to Beer, the well where the LORD said to Moses, “Gather the people so that I may give them water.” (21:16).
Then Israel sang this song: “Spring up, O well, all of you sing to it! (21:17).
The princes dug the well; the nobles of the people hollowed it out with their scepters and with their staffs.” From the wilderness the Israelites went on to Mattanah, (21:18).
and from Mattanah to Nahaliel, and from Nahaliel to Bamoth, (21:19).
and from Bamoth to the valley in Moab where the top of Pisgah overlooks the wasteland. (21:20).
Then Israel sent messengers to Sihon king of the Amorites, saying, (21:21).

“Let us pass through your land. We will not turn aside into any field or vineyard, or drink water from any well. We will stay on the King’s Highway until we have passed through your territory.” (21:22).

But Sihon would not let Israel pass through his territory. Instead, he gathered his whole army and went out to confront Israel in the wilderness. When he came to Jahaz, he fought against Israel. (21:23).
And Israel put him to the sword and took possession of his land, from the Arnon to the Jabbok — but only up to the border of the Ammonites, because it was fortified. (21:24).
Israel captured all the cities of the Amorites and occupied them, including Heshbon and all its villages. (21:25).
Heshbon was the city of Sihon king of the Amorites, who had fought against the former king of Moab and taken all his land as far as the Arnon. (21:26).
That is why the poets say: “Come to Heshbon, let it be rebuilt; let the city of Sihon be restored. (21:27).
For a fire went out from Heshbon, a blaze from the city of Sihon. It consumed Ar of Moab, the rulers of Arnon’s heights. (21:28).
Woe to you, O Moab! You are destroyed, O people of Chemosh! He gave up his sons as refugees, and his daughters into captivity to Sihon king of the Amorites. (21:29).
But we have overthrown them; Heshbon is destroyed as far as Dibon. We demolished them as far as Nophah, which reaches to Medeba.” (21:30).
So Israel lived in the land of the Amorites. (21:31).
After Moses had sent spies to Jazer, Israel captured its villages and drove out the Amorites who were there. (21:32).
Then they turned and went up the road to Bashan, and Og king of Bashan and his whole army came out to meet them in battle at Edrei. (21:33).

But the LORD said to Moses, “Do not fear him, for I have delivered him into your hand, along with all his people and his land. Do to him as you did to Sihon king of the Amorites, who lived in Heshbon.” (21:34).
So they struck down Og, along with his sons and his whole army, until no remnant was left. And they took possession of his land. (21:35).
crossRefs: 2 Kings 18:4: Hezekiah breaks the bronze serpent in pieces, because Israel had been burning incense to it.
John 3:14-15: As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up.
Deuteronomy 2:26-37: The request to Sihon and the taking of Heshbon told again by Moses.
Deuteronomy 3:1-11: Og of Bashan defeated at Edrei, with his iron bedstead measured at nine cubits by four.
Jeremiah 48:45-46: Jeremiah quotes the Heshbon ballad back against Moab, woe to you, people of Chemosh.

translationNotes.note: To place under the ban: everything taken is handed over irrevocably and nothing is kept as plunder. Israel vows it here against Arad, and the place is renamed Hormah from the same root (21:3). Achan's theft at Jericho is a breach of exactly this (Joshua 7:1), and Saul's failure to carry it out against Amalek costs him the kingdom (1 Samuel 15).

The Hebrew calls them burning ones, the same word used of the winged beings in Isaiah 6:2. The name most likely describes the effect: the burn of the venom in the wound. Isaiah 30:6 speaks of the flying seraph among the animals of the Negev. Venomous snakes are still a genuine hazard of that country, and the text presents this as an ordinary danger sent as a judgment, not a new species.

The two Hebrew words are almost the same sound: a nachash of nechoshet, a snake of copper. English cannot carry it. Something very like this object has been found: a copper serpent about twelve centimetres long with a gilded head, excavated by Beno Rothenberg in a Midianite tent shrine at the Timna copper mines in the Arabah. Israel kept Moses' serpent for centuries and eventually burned incense to it, until Hezekiah destroyed it and called it Nehushtan, a mere bit of bronze (2 Kings 18:4).

translationNotes.term: The Book of the Wars of the LORD
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: סֵפֶר מִלְחֲמֹת יְהוָה (Sefer Milchamot YHWH)
translationNotes.note: A written source quoted at verse 14 and not preserved anywhere else. Scripture cites other such collections by name: the Book of Jashar (Joshua 10:13; 2 Samuel 1:18) and the annals of the kings of Israel and Judah. This chapter quotes three separate pieces of older poetry, this one, the Song of the Well (21:17-18) and the ballad of Heshbon (21:27-30), and marks each as a quotation.

The Arnon, today the Wadi Mujib, cuts a canyon roughly half a kilometre deep across the plateau east of the Dead Sea, and it formed the border between Moab to the south and the Amorites to the north (21:13). Verse 26 explains the politics: Sihon had already taken the land north of it from a previous king of Moab, so when Israel takes it from Sihon it is not taking Moabite land, which Israel was forbidden to do (Deuteronomy 2:9).

The national god of Moab, named in the quoted ballad at verse 29, which calls the Moabites the people of Chemosh. His worship included human sacrifice: 2 Kings 3:27 records the king of Moab offering his own eldest son as a burnt offering on the city wall to break a siege. The Moabite Stone, a victory inscription of King Mesha found at Dhiban in 1868 and dating to about 840 BC, credits Chemosh with Moab's victories throughout and describes putting a captured town to the ban for him.

stories.keyTakeaway: Israel defeats the Canaanite king of Arad after vowing to destroy his cities, then travels through the wilderness where they complain and are struck by venomous snakes until Moses makes a bronze snake for healing. They continue east, defeat Sihon king of the Amorites and take his land, then defeat Og king of Bashan and occupy his territory as well.

stories.title: 🐍 Numbers 22
summaryBullets: Then the Israelites traveled on and camped in the plains of Moab near the Jordan, across from Jericho. (22:1).
Now Balak son of Zippor saw all that Israel had done to the Amorites, (22:2).
and Moab was terrified of the people because they were numerous. Indeed, Moab dreaded the Israelites. (22:3).
So the Moabites said to the elders of Midian, “This horde will devour everything around us, as an ox licks up the grass of the field.” Since Balak son of Zippor was king of Moab at that time, (22:4).

he sent messengers to summon Balaam son of Beor at Pethor, which is by the Euphrates in the land of his people. “Behold, a people has come out of Egypt,” said Balak. “They cover the face of the land and have settled next to me. (22:5).

So please come now and put a curse on this people, because they are too mighty for me. Perhaps I may be able to defeat them and drive them out of the land; for I know that those you bless are blessed, and those you curse are cursed.” (22:6).
The elders of Moab and Midian departed with the fees for divination in hand. They came to Balaam and relayed to him the words of Balak. (22:7).
“Spend the night here,” Balaam replied, “and I will give you the answer that the LORD speaks to me.” So the princes of Moab stayed with Balaam. (22:8).
Then God came to Balaam and asked, “Who are these men with you?” (22:9).
And Balaam said to God, “Balak son of Zippor, king of Moab, sent me this message: (22:10).
‘Behold, a people has come out of Egypt, and they cover the face of the land. Now come and put a curse on them for me. Perhaps I may be able to fight against them and drive them away.’” (22:11).
But God said to Balaam, “Do not go with them. You are not to curse this people, for they are blessed.” (22:12).
So Balaam got up the next morning and said to Balak’s princes, “Go back to your homeland, because the LORD has refused to let me go with you.” (22:13).
And the princes of Moab arose, returned to Balak, and said, “Balaam refused to come with us.” (22:14).
Then Balak sent other princes, more numerous and more distinguished than the first messengers. (22:15).
They came to Balaam and said, “This is what Balak son of Zippor says: ‘Please let nothing hinder you from coming to me, (22:16).
for I will honor you richly and do whatever you say. So please come and put a curse on this people for me!’” (22:17).
But Balaam replied to the servants of Balak, “If Balak were to give me his house full of silver and gold, I could not do anything small or great to go beyond the command of the LORD my God. (22:18).
So now, please stay here overnight as the others did, that I may find out what else the LORD has to tell me.” (22:19).
That night God came to Balaam and said, “Since these men have come to summon you, get up and go with them, but you must only do what I tell you.” (22:20).
So in the morning Balaam got up, saddled his donkey, and went with the princes of Moab. (22:21).
Then God’s anger was kindled because Balaam was going along, and the angel of the LORD stood in the road to oppose him. Balaam was riding his donkey, and his two servants were with him. (22:22).
When the donkey saw the angel of the LORD standing in the road with a drawn sword in his hand, she turned off the path and went into a field. So Balaam beat her to return her to the path. (22:23).
Then the angel of the LORD stood in a narrow passage between two vineyards, with walls on either side. (22:24).
And the donkey saw the angel of the LORD and pressed herself against the wall, crushing Balaam’s foot against it. So he beat her once again. (22:25).
And the angel of the LORD moved on ahead and stood in a narrow place where there was no room to turn to the right or left. (22:26).
When the donkey saw the angel of the LORD, she lay down under Balaam, and he became furious and beat her with his staff. (22:27).
Then the LORD opened the donkey’s mouth, and she said to Balaam, “What have I done to you that you have beaten me these three times?” (22:28).
Balaam answered the donkey, “You have made a fool of me! If I had a sword in my hand, I would kill you right now!” (22:29).
But the donkey said to Balaam, “Am I not the donkey you have ridden all your life until today? Have I ever treated you this way before?” “No,” he replied. (22:30).
Then the LORD opened Balaam’s eyes, and he saw the angel of the LORD standing in the road with a drawn sword in his hand. And Balaam bowed low and fell facedown. (22:31).
The angel of the LORD asked him, “Why have you beaten your donkey these three times? Behold, I have come out to oppose you, because your way is perverse before me. (22:32).
The donkey saw me and turned away from me these three times. If she had not turned away, then by now I would surely have killed you and let her live.” (22:33).

“I have sinned,” Balaam said to the angel of the LORD, “for I did not realize that you were standing in the road to confront me. And now, if this is displeasing in your sight, I will go back home.” (22:34).
But the angel of the LORD said to Balaam, “Go with the men, but you are to speak only what I tell you.” So Balaam went with the princes of Balak. (22:35).
When Balak heard that Balaam was coming, he went out to meet him at the Moabite city on the Arnon border, at the edge of his territory. (22:36).
And he said to Balaam, “Did I not send you an urgent summons? Why did you not come to me? Am I really not able to reward you richly?” (22:37).
“See, I have come to you,” Balaam replied, “but can I say just anything? I must speak only the word that God puts in my mouth.” (22:38).
So Balaam accompanied Balak, and they came to Kiriath-huzoth. (22:39).
Balak sacrificed cattle and sheep, and he gave portions to Balaam and the princes who were with him. (22:40).
The next morning, Balak took Balaam and brought him up to Bamoth-baal. From there he could see the outskirts of the camp of the people. (22:41).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 23:3-5: No Ammonite or Moabite may enter the assembly, because they hired Balaam against Israel.
Joshua 24:9-10: Balak fought Israel and summoned Balaam, but I would not listen to him, and he blessed you instead.
2 Peter 2:15-16: Balaam loved the wages of wickedness and was rebuked by a donkey speaking with a man's voice.
Genesis 19:36-37: Moab is born to Lot's elder daughter, the origin of the nation Balak rules.
Genesis 25:1-2: Midian is born to Abraham by Keturah, the people whose elders come to Balak's council.

translationNotes.note: Moab holds the plateau east of the Dead Sea between the Arnon gorge and the Zered, and its people descend from Lot (Genesis 19:36-37). Israel had just destroyed Sihon and Og, the two kingdoms directly to Moab's north, and was now camped along Moab's border in numbers Moab could not fight. Verses 3 and 4 give the calculation exactly: dread of a force that will eat up everything around it like an ox licking up grass.

Moab is a settled kingdom; Midian is a confederation of desert clans ranging northwest Arabia and Transjordan, descended from Abraham by Keturah (Genesis 25:1-2). Moab approaches them because the two shared that frontier and because Midianite clans could move where an army could not. This alliance is why chapters 25 and 31 end with Midian, and 31:8 names five Midianite kings killed with Balaam.

A professional diviner summoned from Pethor by the Euphrates, hundreds of miles away, which is a measure of his reputation and of what Balak was willing to spend. His name and his father's turn up outside the Bible: at Tell Deir Alla in the Jordan valley, a team led by Henk Franken found in 1967 an inscription written in ink on wall plaster, dated to roughly 800 BC, that opens by naming Balaam son of Beor, a seer of the gods.

The delegation arrives carrying the payment in hand (22:7). Divination was a paid profession across the ancient Near East, with priests reading livers, oil on water, the flight of birds and the stars, and clay models of sheep livers marked with omen readings survive from Mesopotamia. Israel's law forbids the whole trade outright (Deuteronomy 18:10-12), which is why Balaam is a foreign specialist and not a prophet of Israel.

translationNotes.term: The angel of the LORD with a drawn sword
translationNotes.note: The same figure with the same drawn sword meets Joshua outside Jericho (Joshua 5:13) and stands over Jerusalem in David's day (1 Chronicles 21:16). A drawn sword in the road is a soldier blocking a route, and that is what the donkey keeps trying to get around: an open field first, then a walled lane between vineyards, then a place too narrow to pass. The animal sees the obstacle at three narrowing points and the professional seer sees nothing.

stories.keyTakeaway: Balak king of Moab hires the diviner Balaam to curse Israel, but God forbids it; after Balaam changes his mind and sets out anyway, God's angel blocks his path until the donkey speaks and Balaam sees the angel, then he agrees to speak only God's words. Balak meets Balaam and takes him to Bamoth Baal to view the Israelite camp.

stories.title: 🐍 Numbers 23
summaryBullets: Then Balaam said to Balak, “Build for me seven altars here, and prepare for me seven bulls and seven rams.” (23:1).
So Balak did as Balaam had instructed, and Balak and Balaam offered a bull and a ram on each altar. (23:2).

“Stay here by your burnt offering while I am gone,” Balaam said to Balak. “Perhaps the LORD will meet with me. And whatever He reveals to me, I will tell you.” So Balaam went off to a barren height, (23:3).
and God met with him. “I have set up seven altars,” Balaam said, “and on each altar I have offered a bull and a ram.” (23:4).
Then the LORD put a message in Balaam’s mouth, saying, “Return to Balak and give him this message.” (23:5).
So he returned to Balak, who was standing there beside his burnt offering, with all the princes of Moab. (23:6).
And Balaam lifted up an oracle, saying: “Balak brought me from Aram, the king of Moab from the mountains of the east. ‘Come,’ he said, ‘put a curse on Jacob for me; come and denounce Israel!’ (23:7).
How can I curse those whom God has not cursed? How can I denounce those whom the LORD has not denounced? (23:8).
For I see them from atop the rocky cliffs, and I watch them from the hills. Behold, a people dwelling apart, not reckoning themselves among the nations. (23:9).
Who can count the dust of Jacob or number even a fourth of Israel? Let me die the death of the righteous; let my end be like theirs!” (23:10).
Then Balak said to Balaam, “What have you done to me? I brought you here to curse my enemies, and behold, you have only blessed them!” (23:11).
But Balaam replied, “Should I not speak exactly what the LORD puts in my mouth?” (23:12).
Then Balak said to him, “Please come with me to another place where you can see them. You will only see the outskirts of their camp — not all of them. And from there, curse them for me.” (23:13).
So Balak took him to the field of Zophim, to the top of Pisgah, where he built seven altars and offered a bull and a ram on each altar. (23:14).
Balaam said to Balak, “Stay here beside your burnt offering while I meet the LORD over there.” (23:15).
And the LORD met with Balaam and put a message in his mouth, saying, “Return to Balak and speak what I tell you.” (23:16).
So he returned to Balak, who was standing there by his burnt offering with the princes of Moab. “What did the LORD say?” Balak asked. (23:17).
Then Balaam lifted up an oracle, saying: “Arise, O Balak, and listen; give ear to me, O son of Zippor. (23:18).
God is not a man, that He should lie, or a son of man, that He should change His mind. Does He speak and not act? Does He promise and not fulfill? (23:19).
I have indeed received a command to bless; He has blessed, and I cannot change it. (23:20).
He considers no disaster for Jacob; He sees no trouble for Israel. The LORD their God is with them, and the shout of the King is among them. (23:21).
God brought them out of Egypt with strength like a wild ox. (23:22).
For there is no spell against Jacob and no divination against Israel. It will now be said of Jacob and Israel, ‘What great things God has done!’ (23:23).
Behold, the people rise like a lioness; they rouse themselves like a lion, not resting until they devour their prey and drink the blood of the slain.” (23:24).
Now Balak said to Balaam, “Then neither curse them at all nor bless them at all!” (23:25).
But Balaam replied, “Did I not tell you that whatever the LORD says, I must do?” (23:26).
“Please come,” said Balak, “I will take you to another place. Perhaps it will please God that you curse them for me from there.” (23:27).
And Balak took Balaam to the top of Peor, which overlooks the wasteland. (23:28).
Then Balaam said, “Build for me seven altars here, and prepare for me seven bulls and seven rams.” (23:29).
So Balak did as Balaam had instructed, and he offered a bull and a ram on each altar. (23:30).
crossRefs: Numbers 22:38: Balaam has already told Balak he can speak only the word God puts in his mouth.
1 Samuel 15:29: The Glory of Israel does not lie or change His mind, the same claim as Numbers 23:19.
Genesis 12:3: I will bless those who bless you, and whoever curses you I will curse.
Genesis 13:16: I will make your offspring like the dust of the earth, so that they cannot be counted.
Deuteronomy 18:10-12: No one among you shall practise divination, interpret omens, or cast spells.

translationNotes.term: Seven altars, seven bulls, seven rams
translationNotes.note: Balaam sets this up three separate times, at three different sites (23:1,14,29). Seven is the standard number for a complete set in ritual across the region, and building altars on a height in view of the target was standard divination practice: the seer needed to see what he was cursing, which is why Balak keeps moving him to new viewpoints in verses 13 and 27.

A mashal is a formal saying, and the word covers proverbs, taunt songs and figured speech; the book of Proverbs takes its Hebrew title from it. It is not the ordinary word for a prophecy. Each of Balaam's utterances is introduced with it, marking them as crafted formal poetry rather than conversation.

An open-air worship platform, usually on a hilltop or ridge, with an altar and often a standing stone and a wooden pole. Balak's three sites are Bamoth-baal, the high places of Baal (22:41), the field of Zophim on Pisgah, and the top of Peor. Excavated examples have been found at Megiddo and Dan. These are working sanctuaries of the Moabite cult, and Balak is bringing Balaam to his own gods' ground.

Verse 23 names the two main branches of the trade: nachash, reading omens, and qesem, casting lots or arrows to obtain a decision. Ezekiel 21:21 shows a Babylonian king doing both at a crossroads, shaking arrows, consulting images and inspecting a liver. Balaam is announcing that his entire profession has no purchase here.

The aurochs, the wild ancestor of cattle, standing about 1.8 metres at the shoulder, hunted by kings across the ancient Near East and surviving in Europe until 1627. It was the proverbial untameable strength. The Greek Old Testament rendered the word monokeros, one-horn, and that is how unicorn came into older English Bibles at this verse and at Job 39:9.

stories.keyTakeaway: Balaam attempts three times to curse Israel for Balak, but God compels him to bless Israel instead each time, declaring their strength and protection despite Balak's mounting frustration.

stories.title: 🐍 Numbers 24
summaryBullets: And when Balaam saw that it pleased the LORD to bless Israel, he did not seek omens as on previous occasions, but he turned his face toward the wilderness. (24:1).
When Balaam looked up and saw Israel encamped tribe by tribe, the Spirit of God came upon him, (24:2).
and he lifted up an oracle, saying: “This is the prophecy of Balaam son of Beor, the prophecy of a man whose eyes are open, (24:3).
the prophecy of one who hears the words of God, who sees a vision from the Almighty, who bows down with eyes wide open: (24:4).
How lovely are your tents, O Jacob, your dwellings, O Israel! (24:5).
They spread out like palm groves, like gardens beside a stream, like aloes the LORD has planted, like cedars beside the waters. (24:6).
Water will flow from his buckets, and his seed will have abundant water. His king will be greater than Agag, and his kingdom will be exalted. (24:7).
God brought him out of Egypt with strength like a wild ox, to devour hostile nations and crush their bones, to pierce them with arrows. (24:8).
He crouches, he lies down like a lion, like a lioness— who dares to rouse him? Blessed are those who bless you and cursed are those who curse you.” (24:9).

Then Balak’s anger burned against Balaam, and he struck his hands together and said to Balaam, “I summoned you to curse my enemies, but behold, you have persisted in blessing them these three times. (24:10).
Therefore , flee at once to your home! I said I would reward you richly, but instead the LORD has denied your reward.” (24:11).
Balaam answered Balak, “Did I not already tell the messengers you sent me (24:12).

that even if Balak were to give me his house full of silver and gold, I could not do anything of my own accord, good or bad, to go beyond the command of the LORD? I must speak whatever the LORD says. (24:13).
Now I am going back to my people, but come, let me warn you what this people will do to your people in the days to come.” (24:14).
Then Balaam lifted up an oracle, saying, “This is the prophecy of Balaam son of Beor, the prophecy of a man whose eyes are open, (24:15).
the prophecy of one who hears the words of God, who has knowledge from the Most High, who sees a vision from the Almighty, who bows down with eyes wide open: (24:16).

I see him, but not now; I behold him, but not near. A star will come forth from Jacob, and a scepter will arise from Israel. He will crush the skulls of Moab and strike down all the sons of Sheth. (24:17).
Edom will become a possession, as will Seir, his enemy; but Israel will perform with valor. (24:18).
A ruler will come from Jacob and destroy the survivors of the city.” (24:19).
Then Balaam saw Amalek and lifted up an oracle, saying: “Amalek was first among the nations, but his end is destruction.” (24:20).
Next he saw the Kenites and lifted up an oracle, saying: “Your dwelling place is secure, and your nest is set in a cliff. (24:21).
Yet Kain will be destroyed when Asshur takes you captive.” (24:22).
Once more Balaam lifted up an oracle, saying: “Ah, who can live unless God has ordained it? (24:23).
Ships will come from the coasts of Cyprus; they will subdue Asshur and Eber, but they too will perish forever.” (24:24).
Then Balaam arose and returned to his homeland, and Balak also went on his way. (24:25).
crossRefs: Genesis 49:9-10: Judah is a lion's cub, and the sceptre will not depart from Judah.
Matthew 2:1-2: Wise men from the east arrive saying they have seen His star and have come to worship Him.
Revelation 22:16: I am the Root and the Offspring of David, the bright Morning Star.
Exodus 17:8-16: Amalek attacks Israel at Rephidim, and war against Amalek is declared from generation to generation.
Judges 1:16: The descendants of the Kenite, Moses' father-in-law, go up with the men of Judah into the wilderness.

translationNotes.note: Verse 1 records the change of method: for the first two oracles Balaam went off to look for omens, and this time he does not. The narrator states it flatly, as a change in professional procedure. What follows is introduced as the Spirit of God coming on him, which is the only place in the book that phrase is used of Balaam.

The phrase occurs only in Balaam's two self-descriptions (24:3,15) and its exact sense is not settled; it has been read as the open eye and as the closed eye, that is, a man who sees with his eyes shut. Either way it is the language of a professional seer describing his own credentials, and the verses around it stack four more: he hears the words of God, has knowledge from the Most High, sees a vision from the Almighty, and falls with eyes uncovered.

A sceptre is the rod a king holds, so the pair means a ruler rising out of Jacob. Genesis 49:10 uses the same word for Judah's rule. This is a foreign diviner, hired to curse, delivering a line about a coming king of Israel, and the text presents it as what he was made to say. Matthew 2:2 has men from the east arriving in Jerusalem because of a star.

A clan associated with Midian; Moses' father-in-law is called both a priest of Midian and a Kenite (Exodus 3:1; Judges 1:16). They lived in the rocky country of the Negev and Sinai, and their name is close to the Hebrew word for a metalworker, which fits a people living near the copper mining districts. Verse 21 puns on that: your nest is set in the rock, where qen, nest, sounds like their name.

translationNotes.term: Ships from the coasts of Cyprus
translationNotes.note: Kittim takes its name from Kition, a Phoenician city on Cyprus, and the term widened to mean the sea peoples and later the powers coming from the west; Daniel 11:30 uses it of a fleet that turns back a Seleucid king, and the Dead Sea Scrolls use it of Rome. Verse 24 is the last thing Balaam says, and it is about ships arriving from across the sea to break the great land powers.

stories.keyTakeaway: Balaam, compelled by God's Spirit, blesses Israel four times despite Balak's fury, praising their strength and predicting their future dominance over Moab, Edom, Amalek, and other nations. Balaam then returns home, explaining he could only speak what the Lord commanded.

stories.title: 🐍 Numbers 25
summaryBullets: While Israel was staying in Shittim, the men began to indulge in sexual immorality with the daughters of Moab, (25:1).
who also invited them to the sacrifices for their gods. And the people ate and bowed down to these gods. (25:2).
So Israel joined in worshiping Baal of Peor, and the anger of the LORD burned against them. (25:3).
Then the LORD said to Moses, “Take all the leaders of the people and execute them in broad daylight before the LORD, so that His fierce anger may turn away from Israel.” (25:4).
